Welcome to Aftermarket Report, a newsletter where we do a quick daily wrap-up of what happened in the markets, both in India and globally.
In our latest episode of I n The Money by Zerodha , we get into the part guides treat as an afterthought – stock selection. Not a checklist, not a screener dump. A method.
Specifically, the Wagner and Pedicelli approach: find the strongest stock inside the strongest sector, and let the money flows do the heavy lifting.
We walk through two live examples using NSE sectoral indexes and the TJI sub-sector indexes, and share a custom TradingView script that builds a true equal-weighted basket — because market-cap weighting lies to you about what’s actually moving. One thing worth flagging before you dive in: discretionary doesn’t mean no rules. It never has.

A sharp but short-lived spike above 24,020 in the final 30 minutes quickly fizzled out as selling returned. Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella coined a new term, "The Reverse Information Paradox":
As enterprises continue using AI models over time, the information asymmetry becomes increasingly skewed. The seller learns more and more about the buyer through prompts, interactions, and usage, while the buyer learns very little about what the seller is learning in return.
“Models learn from exhaust, the prompts people write, the tools agents use, and especially the corrections people make when the model is wrong. Every correction is distilled into institutional know-how. It’s the kind of knowledge a competitor could never buy, and the kind that leaks almost imperceptibly: trace by trace, correction by correction, eval by eval,”
“In consuming intelligence, you are creating intelligence. And what you create should belong to you.” - Link

Hi, I’m Kashish and sometime towards the end of May, Amit Tripathi said something on CNBC that I couldn’t let go of.
Source
Some of India’s largest, safest, AAA-rated banks — the SBIs and HDFCs of the world — were raising three-month money at 7.25% to 7.75%. At the same time, the RBI’s repo rate, the anchor the entire interest-rate system is supposed to hang off, was sitting at 5.25%. That is a spread of 225 basis points — 2.25% — over the policy rate, just to borrow for ninety days. And as Amit put it, spreads like that don’t turn up when things are fine. Historically, they turn up in the middle of a crisis.
It was a dense, throwaway line on a business channel that most people would nod along to and forget. But it’s the kind of statement that, if you pull on it, unspools into almost everything: how banks actually pay for themselves, why the money they raise has quietly gotten more expensive, what liquidity really does, why the RBI reached out to non-resident Indians a week later, and why the business of banking in India may be about to change shape.
So I did the only sensible thing. I got Amit — three decades in India’s capital markets, the last two at Nippon, currently its CIO for fixed income — to sit down and let me bother him about that one sentence until it made sense.
The full conversation is on our YouTube Channel or if you like listening, you can check out Spotify or Apple podcasts .
Below is an edited version of the transcript, with my own highlights in bold. If you’d rather not read the whole thing, here are the bits that stuck with me.
In late May, India’s biggest AAA banks were paying 225 basis points over the repo rate for three-month money. That spread almost never appears outside a market or macro dislocation.
The repo rate isn’t really how banks fund themselves. It’s collateralised, temporary, and capped by how few government bonds a bank actually holds. You cannot run a balance sheet off the repo window.
Liquidity, not the repo rate, is what actually sets borrowing costs in the economy. A low policy rate means nothing if there’s no cash in the system.
“Credit creates its own deposits” — but only in a closed system. India leaks money out through oil imports and foreign outflows, and that leak is what broke the link this time.
The RBI’s move to court NRI deposits a week later wasn’t a coincidence. And it’s the government, not just the RBI, that quietly foots the bill.
The cheap deposits banks have leaned on for decades are structurally shrinking. Amit thinks securitisation is coming back as a core tool over the next three to five years.
A spread that only shows up when things break
Kashish: The thing that stood out in your CNBC interview was one line — banks paying 225 basis points over the repo rate for three-month money. It’s a very dense statement. Can you just explain it simply, and then we’ll drill into the pieces?
Amit: Towards the end of May, AAA PSU banks and AAA private banks — some of the largest banks in this country — were raising three-month money, both as wholesale deposits and through certificates of deposit, at rates in the range of 7.25% to 7.75%. Compare that with the RBI’s policy rate, the repo rate, which was at 5.25% at the same time.
So for a bank to borrow three-month money at 2% or more over the policy rate, just for ninety days, is not normal in any cycle we’ve seen in India for many years. The few times it has happened, it has happened in the midst of a market dysfunction, or a macro or micro crisis. These kinds of spreads are only available when things are not well. Otherwise they’re not.
So the statement was simply to suggest that while everything on the face of it looks reasonably well placed, there are sections that have faced pressure over the last couple of quarters — and that pressure was showing up in the rates at which banks were borrowing.
This is the whole piece in miniature. A number that looks technical is really a stress signal, and the rest of the conversation is Amit walking me through what was pressing on it.
What the repo rate actually is — and isn’t
Kashish: Let me ask a stupid question. If the repo rate is, by definition, the rate at which banks can borrow from the RBI, why don’t banks just take all their money from the RBI? Why go outside and pay a 2.25% spread at all?
Amit: I’m going to partly step into the banking domain, which isn’t mine, so some banker will hear this and forgive me. But let me try.
Repo is just short for repurchase. Every central bank in the world manages monetary policy around a fulcrum, and that fulcrum is the policy rate. It’s meant to guide the market on where the risk-free, one-day borrowing and lending should happen.
Two things about it. First, it’s a policy rate — a signal. By setting it, the RBI is telling the market where a neutral, overnight, collateralised lending rate should sit. If you came to me tomorrow and asked me to lend to you against the same government collateral the RBI accepts, I’d charge you something close to that rate, because that’s the established reference.
Second, it’s a collateralised facility, not free money. A bank has to pledge securities — mostly government bonds — to the RBI to borrow for a day, seven days, fourteen days. So it’s already holding the collateral; it’s just taking temporary funding against it. Repo was never designed as a permanent form of borrowing. And banks hold very limited sovereign collateral relative to their whole balance sheet. You can in no way fund a balance sheet through the repo window alone. You need many other instruments to raise money.
How a bank actually pays for itself
Amit: Look at the liability side of any bank — how it raises money. Like any company, it has two sources: equity and borrowings. But because a bank’s business is borrowing and lending, borrowings dominate.
And there are many kinds. The current account money you keep with a bank is a borrowing for the bank. So is your savings balance, your fixed deposit, the money someone lends against a certificate of deposit, the infrastructure bonds it issues. There are even quasi-equity borrowings, like tier-two and perpetual debt — but let’s not go there.
Here’s what matters. Over the last ten to twenty years, the cheapest money available to banks — current and savings account balances, what we call CASA — has been shrinking as a share, and the higher-cost money, term deposits and wholesale certificates of deposit, has been growing. In a savings account you might earn 2.5% or 3%. Put a fixed deposit with the same bank and it’ll give you 7%. So as the mix tilts from CASA towards fixed and wholesale deposits, the bank’s overall cost of funding simply goes up. That’s why, when you read bank results, the CASA ratio they report has been drifting down. That’s the pressure on cost of funds, hiding in plain sight.
Credit creates its own deposits — until India springs a leak
Kashish: So where does that pressure come from right now?
Amit: Two things came together. One, credit growth. In the last twelve to eighteen months, especially after the GST reforms around September 2025, credit growth picked up sharply — consumer credit, auto, credit cards, personal loans, gold loans. The banks’ asset books have been growing fast, and they have to fund that growth with liabilities.
Now, a small technical point I’ll ask you to take at face value: credit creates its own deposits. If I lend money to you, you park it in a bank, or you pay a supplier who parks it in a bank. The money doesn’t vanish. So when credit growth picks up, deposit growth follows — with a lag.
But that’s only true in a closed loop. Imagine India as a sealed system where no money enters or leaves. Then it doesn’t matter how fast credit grows, because deposits mechanically keep pace. The problem is that India isn’t a closed system. We import oil, foreign investors pull money out — net money leaves the country. That’s the current account deficit, the balance-of-payments deficit. And that money leaving does not come back as a deposit in an Indian bank. Somebody has to replace it, and that somebody is ultimately the RBI, by putting fresh money into the system.
This was the part that reframed the whole thing for me. The “225 over repo” number wasn’t really about banks being greedy or reckless. It was the domestic symptom of an external problem — money leaking out faster than the credit-deposit machine could refill it.
Amit: So over the last year and a half, credit growth picked up on one side while the external sector turned more negative on the other — foreign outflows, higher oil prices. Put together, you get temporary bouts of tight cash, even though the RBI has pumped in a record amount. Just last year it did about ₹8 lakh crore of open market operations — buying bonds from banks and handing them cash in return.
And here’s the deeper worry. Every credit cycle problem tends to begin as a macro problem and then convert into a micro one. A modern economy runs on the smooth delivery of credit at reasonable prices to deserving borrowers. You never want a temporary macro disturbance to harden into a situation where credit itself becomes scarce or expensive. That channel is what you guard against — which is why you solve the macro fast.
Why the RBI reached out to NRIs
Kashish: And a week after your statement, the RBI made the FCNR announcement. Can you explain how that solves the problem?
Amit: Banks can raise deposits from many sources, including non-residents — and NRIs are an enormous source of funding for India. Every year we get more than a hundred billion dollars in repatriation; last year it was over $130 billion.
But an NRI weighing a rupee deposit doesn’t just look at the interest rate. He also holds money abroad in dollars, and he worries about the rupee depreciating over the life of the deposit. If he expects the rupee to weaken, say, 10% against the dollar, he wants to be compensated for that too — so the rate a bank would have to offer him gets pushed uncomfortably high.
What the RBI did was step in and absorb the currency-depreciation cost. So if SBI offers a 6% deposit, the RBI effectively covers the depreciation compensation on top. That does two things at once. It satisfies the NRI, who no longer carries the currency worry. And it lets the bank borrow much larger sums at a competitive rate — because if the bank had to fund both the deposit rate and the depreciation cover itself, the all-in cost would have been far higher.
So it hits the micro problem — credit growth getting funded by deposits — and the macro problem, because those dollars come into India and shore up our foreign exchange reserves.
Kashish: So it’s a clean fix.
Amit: It’s a timely one. But is it a fundamental solution? No. You’re buying time, because it’s borrowed money, and someone is bearing a cost. And here’s the part people miss: that cost sits with the RBI, which is just an arm of the government. The RBI pays its surplus to the government as dividend, so if it’s absorbing this depreciation cost, the dividend shrinks. Please don’t think of monetary policy as separate from fiscal policy. It’s ultimately the government bearing this subsidy so that banks can raise money cheaply and credit keeps flowing.
He then rattled off the fiscal side of the same effort — GST reforms, income-tax cuts, a twenty-year tax holiday for data centres to pull in AI-infrastructure FDI, and zero withholding tax for foreigners buying government bonds. His read: the FCNR window buys a year, and more of these measures will keep coming to repair India’s external balance sheet.
Liquidity beats the repo rate
Kashish: Where do NBFCs fit into all this? Does the repo rate transmit to their cost of funds too?
Amit: An NBFC is just a finance company — it borrows and lends like a bank, minus a few tools like FCNR deposits. But the real point is this: liquidity, not the policy rate, is what determines real interest rates in the economy.
Think of it as a ladder. The lowest-yielding, risk-free asset is a government bond — the 91-day treasury bill, one-year, three-year, thirty-year. That’s the risk-free curve, and the repo rate is its starting point. Everyone else has to pay a spread above it for the risk you take lending to them. So if the government borrows two-year money at 6%, a AAA PSU like NABARD might pay 7.15%, Bajaj Finance 7.6%, a AA name around 8.25%. Everything is built on top of the risk-free rate, and the risk-free rate starts at repo. That’s how the repo rate reaches into every corner of the economy.
But — and this is the key — the RBI doesn’t create loans. Banks and NBFCs do. They lend at X and borrow at Y, and their profit is X minus Y. If Y goes up, X has to follow. So even with the repo rate parked at 5.25%, once banks were borrowing three-month money at 7.5% in May, it was only a matter of time before lending rates rose too.
Kashish: So if there’s surplus liquidity, those expensive three-month rates simply shouldn’t exist? Liquidity lets banks raise money closer to the repo rate?
Amit: Yes. Liquidity is a much bigger driver of short-term borrowing rates than the repo rate itself. Suppose I make liquidity negative and cut the repo rate to 4%. It doesn’t matter — nobody can actually borrow at 4% except from the RBI’s window against government collateral. And in any bank’s balance sheet, no more than about 20 rupees out of every 100 is government securities. The other 80 — car loans, home loans, corporate loans — still has to be funded from the market, and the market needs liquidity to hand over that money.
It’s a double-edged sword, though. Too much liquidity and you get irrational decisions and inflation. So you want adequate surplus — no more.
Kashish: And if the RBI overcorrects and floods the system?
Amit: Temporary surplus is easy to manage — the RBI has plenty of tools. It can absorb one-day money through the SDF, roughly 25 basis points below the repo rate. It can do variable-rate reverse repo to soak up money for longer against collateral. It can sell bonds. So nobody’s worried about mopping up a temporary surplus. What you worry about is core, long-term liquidity staying ample — because that’s what keeps money available at a reasonable price. On top of that, inflation has stayed low and stable for a long time, so even if the RBI hikes, the market expects only two or three moves at most, taking the repo rate to maybe 5.75% or 6%. Limited hikes plus a solid liquidity infusion — that’s what turned market sentiment positive.
What only the capital markets can do
Kashish: We lean heavily on banks for credit creation. In many countries the bond market is far livelier. Could a deeper bond market solve some of India’s credit strain — or is that, too, just a function of liquifdity?
Amit: At the base level, yes, everything eventually comes back to liquidity. But capital markets are a necessary complement to banks, and they’re good at genuinely different things.
Banks are better at origination. Writing a two-wheeler loan, a home loan, an MFI loan in Surat — that needs distribution, thousands of branches, an understanding of borrower risk on the ground. A capital market can’t go originate a lakh of microfinance loans.
But capital markets do other things banks structurally can’t. Long-term infrastructure financing, for one. An insurance company or a pension fund has very long-dated liabilities, so it can fund a thirty-year project without the asset-liability mismatch a bank runs when it funds a thirty-year asset with three-month money. Capital markets also fund the bulk of government borrowing — banks fund around 40% of it, capital markets about 60%.
And then there’s cost. The cost of intermediation in capital markets is far lower than for a bank — not because banks are bad at it, but because a ten-person office in Mumbai has a very different cost structure from a network of thousands of branches. A bank might need a 2.5% to 3% gap between what it borrows and what it lends just to cover its costs. For me, that gap can be as low as 0.25% to 0.5%. That makes the whole system’s lending more efficient — which is exactly why capital markets have to be an integral part of the funding ecosystem.
He kept coming back to one specific fix — a liquid repo market for bonds. His argument: Indians save enormous amounts, and plenty of them would put money into fixed income if they could pledge, say, a Bajaj Finance bond and borrow against it for a couple of months the way a bank pledges bonds to the RBI. Equities pulled money in through returns and tax treatment; bonds never got that pull. Build a well-oiled repo market, and participation follows.
The bank of the future securitises
Kashish: The nature of banking seems to be changing. Banks have funded their loan books with retail deposits, but CASA has fallen structurally over the last five to ten years. If that continues, does banking just become a harder business — higher cost of funds, and you accept it?
Amit: You’ve almost given away that you understand the exact problem. So let me answer properly.
As long as banks had access to cheap CASA and wholesale rates were low and competition was thin, they could just keep growing their balance sheets. That’s changing. So I think both things become true at once — banks keep growing their lending, but they lean far more on capital-market tools like securitisation to do it. One large bank chairman recently said they’ll do more securitisation going forward, including home-loan, or mortgage-backed, securitisation. Interestingly, we actually saw more securitisation between 2005 and 2008 than we do today.
Part of what’s let banks push so hard despite deposit pressure is a good problem: credit costs are among the lowest they’ve ever been. Think of a bank’s economics as lending rate, minus borrowing cost, minus operating cost, minus credit cost — the money lost to bad loans. If credit cost fell from, say, 2% to half a percent, that’s 1.5% of breathing room, and banks have used it to lend aggressively even where their borrowing costs are high.
But this is a good point in the cycle. A bad one will come. So banks will increasingly reach for non-traditional ways to create room on their balance sheets. Picture two banks. One runs a ₹100 balance sheet and earns a 2% return on assets. The other runs a ₹50 balance sheet but earns 3%, because it securitises regularly and keeps churning. As an equity investor, I’d take the smaller, more efficient bank. I see banks getting far more efficient — not just in how they deploy money, but in how they raise it. Securitisation becomes a feature of the system over the next three to five years, even if it isn’t one today.
Kashish: So my conclusion is that banking becomes a genuinely difficult business. The credit cycle turns, fat margins shrink, you can’t just ride CASA anymore, and running a bank gets harder.
Amit: I’d never reach that conclusion. Some of the brightest minds in India run our banks. Banks are going nowhere — they’ll innovate beyond what you or I can imagine. There’s no economy on earth, however developed, where banks don’t have an enormous stake in how the whole thing runs, and that stays true for India.
What I hope is that debt capital markets step up alongside them. The size and needs of this economy are going to explode over the next ten, twenty years. Both have to grow. You cannot run an economy this size on only one of them. The banking system will grow well — the real work is making sure the capital markets grow just as well beside it.

The piece argues that the Supreme Court went wrong in its recent ruling against Kotak Mutual fund [ context here ]. A regulatory philosophy that says outcomes are immaterial cannot govern actors whose defining legal duty is to produce good outcomes.
The Supreme Court’s recent decision in the Kotak mutual fund case has caused unease among not only the mutual fund industry, but across all fund managers, and those who owe a fiduciary duty towards their clients. The term “ fiduciary duty ” can be vague, and varies with the relationship between the person who owes the duty and the person to whom it is owed, but it invariably involves a duty of good faith, trust and honesty. In the specific context of fund managers, it requires them to act in the best interest, and for the benefit of the investors.
Source
Kotak MF launched six close-ended schemes, which were to mature during April to May 2019. Out of the Rs. 1,625 crore collected by the schemes, approximately Rs. 266 crore was invested in debentures of two Essel Group companies. This was secured by pledging shares of Zee Limited, to the tune of 1.5 times of the schemes’ exposure. When Zee’s price collapsed in early 2019 and lenders across the market began invoking their pledges, the cover fell below the agreed level.
At that point, Kotak MF could either enforce its pledge at once, selling a large block of Zee into a falling market and crystallising a loss of approximately Rs. 376 crore for its unitholders, or extend the debentures and pursue an orderly recovery. The former option would have further lowered Zee’s shares, as well as harmed the other lenders, and the latter option, which Kotak MF chose, resulted in profits to the unitholders.
By extending the debentures, the schemes were not wound up on their maturity dates in April to May 2019, resulting in a breach of the Mutual Fund Regulations. Instead, the unitholders were paid in part, and the balance was paid out by September 2019, about 4-5 months after the schemes should have been wound up. After completing its inquiries, SEBI penalised Kotak MF, its senior management, as well as the Trustees. The Securities Appellate Tribunal, while removing certain directions, largely upheld SEBI’s action, which was then affirmed by the Supreme Court as well.
The ultimate decision taken by Kotak MF and its officers is aligned with their fiduciary duties.
The SC relies on investors’ awareness of risk in investing in securities while arriving at its conclusions, and the obligations on Kotak MF under the regulatory framework. Surprisingly, the apex court has missed the central point that Kotak MF was required to act in the best interest, and for the benefit of its unitholders. In fact, the mutual fund regulations mandate that investments are to be taken in the interest of unitholders. Any fiduciary asked to choose between those outcomes on behalf of the people whose money it manages would choose what Kotak MF chose. That is their job.
Per the SC, excusing a profitable breach would incentivise the next one, in a progression from profit to greed and from greed to systemic failure. But this reads conduct backwards, from result to motive. In early 2019 no one knew whether the standstill would hold or collapse. The decision had to be taken under uncertainty, on the information then available, as every investment decision is. A fiduciary who picks the course that appears least harmful to investors, and is later proved right, has not acted out of greed. Prudence is measured before the event, not after it. A court cannot call the outcome immaterial and, in the same breath, read culpability out of it.
The deeper flaw is the assumption that compliance and investor protection always run together. The winding-up rule exists to return unitholders their money on the promised date and to stop a closed scheme carrying open-ended risk. If applied to the letter, Kotak MF would have had to sell Zee’s shares in a collapsing market, resulting in the very harm the framework is intended to avoid. The fund’s fiduciary duty pulled the other way. When a timing rule and the duty it serves point in opposite directions, the investor protection argument is far from puerile. The harshness of the judgment sends a message: it tells a fiduciary that the safe course is mechanical compliance even where compliance would hurt the investor . A regulatory philosophy that says outcomes are immaterial cannot govern actors whose defining legal duty is to produce good outcomes.
The mutual fund regulations do not contemplate a situation where a promoter-pledge structure collapses 90 days before maturity, because regulations cannot contemplate everything. When the unforeseen happens, we rely on fiduciaries to exercise judgment. Instead, the SC announced that it could not examine the commercial prudence of the decision, and then penalised the decision anyway. It refused to weigh the economics while punishing an economic choice.
Kotak MF used neither, and provided SEBI with limited information until it was asked, days after the first schemes had matured. That may not be ideal, but in the absence of a baby-sitter rule, is not a legal breach. A pathway similar to what was implemented by Kotak, which SEBI introduced in 2018, called side-pocketing, was not available to Kotak as it was prospective. In economic terms, what Kotak did was nearly the same. What Kotak did was act in a regulatory vacuum, implementing a solution the regulator itself recognised in 2018. Given the above, attaching personal responsibility to senior functionaries of the manager and the trustee is also over the top regulation. Outcomes cannot be immaterial when they would exonerate and decisive when they condemn. The rules exist to protect the investor, not the other way round.
Sandeep Parekh is the Founder and Managing Partner of Finsec Law Advisors, has taught at IIM Ahmedabad, and served as an Executive Director at SEBI.

The piece uncovers a hidden form of banking fraud where insiders allegedly exploit the trust of NRI and elderly depositors, using fake loans, forged documents, and even cross-bank networks to siphon off fixed deposits. It also asks a tougher question: if banks have modern core banking systems and fraud controls, why do these scams still slip through unnoticed?
It had begun with a casual question.
A non-resident Indian (NRI) customer, visiting her home-branch after two years, noticed something unusual -- a lien mark on one of her term deposits, a deposit she had never pledged for any loan. She had never borrowed from this bank. Not once.
A lien is a legal right or claim that a bank or creditor holds on a customer’s funds, assets, or property to secure the repayment of a debt or financial obligation. When a lien is placed on a bank account, a specific portion of the account balance is temporarily blocked or frozen. The customer can see the money in the total account balance but cannot withdraw, transfer, or spend that locked amount.
What followed was not just the unravelling of a fraud but the uncovering of a cross-bank syndicate – a carefully orchestrated web of colluding employees, forged documents, fictitious loans, and real estate deals. The edifice is built on the silent theft of fixed deposits belonging to those least able to detect it – the NRIs, away for years at a stretch, and elderly citizens, not very familiar with digital banking.
Source
Government data tabled in the Rajya Sabha in early 2026, by Minister of State for Finance Pankaj Chaudhary, reveals that fraud cases, specifically involving bank employees, numbered 1,935 in FY25, down from 2,624 in FY21. The number of such cases dropped further to 400 in the first half of FY26. The decline in reported numbers, however, masks the complexity of such frauds. An IIM Bangalore research paper, citing Reserve Bank of India (RBI) data, says around 34 per cent of banking frauds are internal, attributable to junior and mid-level staff, questioning the integrity, credibility, survivability and processes of the banks.
Let’s get back to the NRI’s case. It’s not an isolated incident; it’s the template of a criminal architecture that had been operating across branches of banks in different geographies for years.
At stage one, a bank staff who has access to the system creates a loan against an NRI’s term deposit, using forged documentation. The original term deposit receipt (TDR) is never discharged. The lien mark exists in the system but the NRI customer is not aware of this.
At stage two, we see the play of an inter-branch rescue game. Before the NRI returns, a second loan is raised in another branch -- this time, targeting a different depositor, and the proceeds are used to close the first loan. The lien is lifted; evidence is buried, and new cheque books are issued from the second account – again without the knowledge of the depositor.
At stage three, the syndicate comes in. When an internal investigation (triggered by a suspicious NRI customer’s complaint) finally traces the money trail, it’s found that a rogue employee is not acting alone. It’s a caucus of staff across multiple banks in the same city, rotating fraudulent loans to cover each other’s tracks. The proceeds are typically used for property deals. Whenever a curious customer asks questions, a new loan from yet another bank arrives to close the trail.
Such “schemes” exploit the trust architecture of banking where branch staff are authorised to renew deposits, assist customers (NRIs or otherwise), and manage elderly account-holders’ paperwork without adequate real-time oversight.
I am not weaving a story. This has been playing out and documented across Indian banks in recent years.
Chennai, 2025: The Central Crime Branch, a specialised, city-level police wing, responsible for investigating complex, organised, and high-profile crimes, arrested 49 bank employees in connection with 18 fraud cases involving forgery, misappropriation, and unauthorised withdrawals. Among the accused were clerks, cashiers, and managers.
Investigators found that bank staff had systematically targeted NRI fixed deposits, with Rs 8 crore siphoned off across multiple NRI accounts using forged signatures and cash vouchers. In one case, the branch manager of a large new private bank fled the country after forging documents to steal Rs 7.5 crore from NRI investments; a Red Corner Notice was subsequently issued.
Mohali, 2025: The branch manager of a public sector bank was booked for securing a Rs93-lakh loan against the fixed deposit of a retired teacher. The fraud came to light when the victim made a routine branch visit -- six months after the unauthorised loan was raised. The accused manager had gradually earned her trust before exploiting it. He was working in conjunction with a real estate agent, confirming the cross-sector conduit that defines the more sophisticated syndicates.
Kota, 2025: A 26-year-old relationship manager of a very large new private bank was arrested for siphoning Rs4.58 crore from over 110 accounts of 41 customers, the majority of which belonged to senior citizens. She operated the fraud over three years (2020–2023), prematurely closing fixed deposits, activating overdraft facilities, and using digital banking to transfer funds to family members’ accounts. The diverted funds were invested in equity derivatives through platforms which buy and sell equities. The bank’s internal audit detected the fraud.
Ahmedabad, 2025: The Enforcement Directorate arrested a PSB executive for fraudulently closing 127 term deposits, public provident fund accounts, senior citizen savings scheme accounts, and current accounts between May 2023 and July 2025, stealing Rs16.10 crore. Victims included senior citizens, deceased account holders, and minors. He was intercepted at a railway station attempting to flee the city.
Haryana, 2024: The manager at a Gurugram branch of the large new private bank (already mentioned) created fake accounts, forged signatures, and manipulated records to siphon Rs16 crore from an NRI woman’s savings account, accumulated over four years. The fraud was discovered only when a new bank employee offered her better FD returns. The customer wanted to shift money from a savings bank account to an FD to earn higher interest but there was no money in her account!
Before core banking solutions (CBS) became the backbone of the system, in the era of handwritten ledgers, incidence of fraud always left physical traces – use of different ink, missing vouchers, inconsistent handwriting. Every entry bore an employee’s initials. Engineering large-scale frauds was structurally difficult. The migration to CBS transformed the game.
The CBS was designed to eliminate manual errors, enable real-time processing, and connect customers seamlessly across branches. It succeeded on all these fronts. But it also has pockets of comfort for the insider-fraudster – almost invisible within the complexity of daily transaction volumes.
The CBS formalised bank transactions but did not formalise oversight proportionally. The system tracks who makes an entry but it doesn’t ask why a particular entry is made. Automated exception reports exist, but their review depends on human beings in an audit chain that is often under-resourced.
The RBI’s revised Master Directions on Fraud Risk Management, issued in July 2024, mandated the creation of special committees of the Board for fraud oversight, deployment of Early Warning Systems (EWS), and a dedicated fraud risk management function at the general manager level or higher.
What the framework still lacks is a mandatory proactive notification system for depositors when any transaction occurs against their term deposit, including lien creation, premature closure, loan creation, or cheque book issuance. For NRI and senior citizen accounts flagged as high trust-risk, a two-factor out-of-band confirmation (SMS/email directly to the depositor’s registered foreign number) before recording any lien, loan or premature closure addresses the vulnerability.
The most alarming dimension of the frauds perpetrated by insiders is their organised, multi-institutional character. Individual rogue employees are manageable within the current framework but when a network of employees across competing banks coordinate, using each other’s institutions as conduits to close loans, launder proceeds, and delay discovery, it’s not easy to crack.
What happens when such frauds are detected? There have been cases of bank staff cooling their heels in jail but one can’t miss the pattern: Detection is accidental, recovery is incomplete, and accountability is diluted – often because banks prefer quiet settlement over criminal prosecution to protect institutional reputation.
What needs to be done to stop this? There could be another column on this on another Monday.
Tamal Bandyopadhyay is a veteran Indian business journalist, accomplished banking author and a Senior Adviser to Jana Small Finance Bank.

Hi folks, I’m Bhuvan , and I’m here to tell you that our newest baby, Subtext , has officially arrived.
Maybe not for those of you who have tuned in early and given us love already. But instead, I’d love to tell you a story of how this baby of ours is hardly new, and has gone through plenty of trials by fire before arriving here.
Subtext started sometime around early 2024 with a piece on that year’s interim budget by Big Pranav (you’ll see why this makes sense), who now makes sure that the well-beloved The Daily Brief (TDB) remains one of the best finance newsletters in India. One idea we cooked up was to start this publication for long-form, in-depth explorations about the weird and wonderful world of finance.
That was version #1 of Subtext, run by just four people: me, Big Pranav, Krishna , and then a few months later, Kashish . Eventually, in the future, we hoped that Subtext would evolve into a platform outside of us where thoughtful people with deep expertise in all things adjacent to markets could write for us.
In the initial days, our Subtext posts averaged north of 2,500 words, and it was a mixed bag where we wrote about all sorts of niches. Those include ticket scalping in Indian concerts , a history of mathematics , finance lessons from the Greek legend of Pandora’s Box , a guest piece by Abid Hassan , and one must-read self-memoir by Big Pranav about how Zerodha messed up by hiring him that — I shit you not — starts with him on a pristine Western toilet. Cinematic stuff, I tell you.
Truly incredible.
Along the way, we had the idea to start a daily newsletter on finance, something akin to a daily newspaper. That eventually became the , under the larger Markets by Zerodha initiative.
With our team size, we couldn’t keep both Subtext and the Daily Brief going at the same time. TDB was, and still is a treadmill, to say the least. We were publishing five newsletters a week while constantly experimenting with other things. Sadly, that forced Subtext to take a backseat, even though I used to publish there occasionally.
Meanwhile, TDB became one of the most popular finance newsletters in India. It is almost like a digital daily for traders, investors, analysts, economists, policymakers, and curious people not just in India, but around the world. That was something we hadn’t really foreseen.
But beyond TDB, the broader Markets by Zerodha umbrella took on a life of its own. Some of our experiments as part of Markets also turned into full-blooded initiatives with their own life.
There’s the , an evening newsletter we publish after the markets close. It summarises the big developments of the day, and what traders and investors should watch out for before the next trading session.
There’s , a newsletter with a cult following of its own. We go through earnings calls, wade through all the corporate boilerplate, and pick out the high-signal things firms say. In the works is also a global-only version of Chatter.
There’s Who Said What , a weekly series where we pick out some of the most interesting comments from the most influential names in business and policy, and then contextualize what they are saying and why.
There’s Points and Figures , our newest initiative, where we tell stories about finance, markets, and the economy using data and high-quality visualizations.
And then there’s In the Money led by the fantastic Sandeep Rao, a channel dedicated to the nitty-gritties of trading strategy.
All of these things now have their own loyal followings. And if I may be a little conceited, I genuinely think they have become the gold standard in their respective arenas.
Once Markets by Zerodha found its footing, though, I told the team that it was time to revive Subtext. And our work in Markets provided direct impetus to that idea.
You see, throughout all our Markets initiatives, we realised that there are so many geeks who have accumulated a phenomenal amount of context about specific sectors, industries, companies, markets, and policies we never knew existed before. Many of these people aren’t well-known outside the specific circles they travel in, but we sincerely believed more people should hear them out. Subtext was meant to platform the work of those people.
But the problem, as those of us writing The Daily Brief know all too well, is that writing is really, really hard. It takes a strange willingness, like a form of self-torture, to sit with your own thoughts and wrestle with them until they stop looking like a half-digested mess, and a lot of experts have day jobs besides writing.
In a pivot, we asked ourselves, instead of asking busy people to write for us, what if we spoke to them? What if we had long, thoughtful conversations with them, recorded those chats, published them as videos and podcasts. And then, hopefully, we could use the transcripts, with LLM assistance, to turn those chats into high-quality articles?
We were also very clear about one thing: we didn’t just want to speak to the same 15–20 people who keep appearing everywhere, saying roughly the same things, in slightly different rooms, with mostly the same microphones. That didn’t really fly with a team that finds it natural to go against the grain.
All of this passion for Subtext remained just that, until LLMs showed up to help us reinvigorate, even modify, those abandoned efforts from the past.
And if you haven’t noticed already, Subtext is already in full swing.
We have already published 14 conversations with policy practitioners, academics, investors, entrepreneurs, and operators who have spent years thinking deeply about the specificities of the Indian and global economy. Some names include: , , Deepak Shenoy , , Rosa Abraham , Zohra Khan and Ajay Srivastava . We thank them for giving our newest baby a chance.
You can find these existing chats on the Markets by Zerodha YouTube channel . But going forward, all new conversations will be published on the new Subtext YouTube channel .
And we’re only getting started. We have a long list of people whose work we’ve learned from and greatly admire. Our plan is to convince them to come on Subtext. We have a pipeline of episodes that we’ve already shot and are in post-production. Our aim is to publish one or two conversations a week. One is a given. Two, we will try. Along with that, every Sunday on Subtext, the Markets team posts what we’re reading that we don’t find space to talk about elsewhere.
Leading the charge on Subtext are Small Pranav (Kumar) ( editor’s note: don’t ask ) and Kashish, who have put immense efforts in everything from guest outreach, to research, to the actual hosting, to social media.
So, to recap, that’s five days of Daily Brief, five days of Aftermarket Report, multiple editions of Chatter during earnings season, Points and Figures, Who Said What, In the Money, plus everything you see on Twitter, Instagram, and LinkedIn — all of that the result of 8-9 people. And now Subtext. Not that we’re complaining.
Much of it owed to the efficiencies borne due to LLMs. Much of it, to smart planning that doesn’t have us burning the midnight oil every single day.
But more than anything, all of this has been possible only because of the love all of you subscribers have shown us. Markets by Zerodha continues to grow from strength to strength only because so many of you keep reading, watching, listening, sharing, criticising, suggesting, and cheering. We thank you the most.
So, yet again, we ask you to give love to another thing we’re trying. Please subscribe to the Subtext YouTube channel if you prefer to get an alert whenever we publish. Hi, I’m Kashish , and I write for The Daily Brief .
Every quarter, listed companies announce their earnings, publish investor presentations, and explain what happened in their business over the last three months. For most people, this can feel overwhelming. And that’s a shame, because these presentations aren’t just for analysts deciding whether to buy or sell a stock. They’re also for curious readers like you and me.
If you know how to read them, they tell you a lot about the pulse of corporate India. They reveal structural shifts, cyclical trends, and the broader health of the economy.
At The Daily Brief, we spend a lot of time trying to make sense of these results for our readers. But we’ve always done it from the perspective of curious outsiders. This earnings season onwards, I wanted to improve that process by talking to someone who has spent years doing this professionally.
That’s when I reached out to Sagar Lele . Over the last decade and a half, he’s worked across financial journalism, sell-side equity research, buy-side fund management, and today is an Executive Director at Paterson Securities.
This conversation was, admittedly, a selfish exercise. The goal wasn’t to predict stocks or find investment ideas. It was to understand how professionals actually read quarterly results, what they pay attention to, what they ignore, and the mental framework they use to separate signal from noise.
Some of the things we talked about stuck with me. I’m sharing seven of them here.
The full conversation is on our YouTube Channel or if you like listening, you can check out Spotify or Apple podcasts .
On why sell-side reports are so long
Retail investors often wonder why brokerages publish fifty-page earnings notes filled with decimal-point projections. Sagar explains that these reports are engineered to serve the very specific needs of buy-side fund managers.
“On the sell side, you are going deep down, you are digging absolutely deep every single detail to the decimal, with an objective of forming a view that assists the buy side in order to make decisions. For a buy side guy, he has to look at the company from the angle of how does it fit in my portfolio? Do I already have the stock or do I not have the stock? Is my other portfolio doing well at this point or not? Sell side reports usually miss this entire context and you can’t personalise it for every fund manager. So your single report has to sort of be as detailed as possible and the buy side will take what is relevant for them from it.”
On tracking cyclical versus structural trends
It is easy to assume that long-term investors do not need to read quarterly results. But Sagar points out that the necessity of tracking earnings quarter-by-quarter depends heavily on whether you are riding a structural wave or playing a cyclical turnaround.
“There are some stocks which are cyclical in nature. If you hold that kind of a stock for a period of seven years, you’ll probably not end up making as much money as trading that cycle. So the efficient way to invest in, even if you’re a long-term investor in cyclical stocks, is to play those cycles because they offer very large deviations between two cycles. On the structural front, I would look at, when I am investing, I would not look into quarterly results too much if the story is already playing out and I’m riding the wave already. Unless something starts falling off the cliff, that’s when I would probably start paying more attention to.”
On cracking valuation expectations
A stock’s price is rarely just a reflection of its underlying business; it is a reflection of what the market expects that business to do. Sagar highlights why understanding the consensus expectation is the hardest, yet most critical, part of investing.
“The price is nothing but a cumulative of expectations. Out of the two components of a target price, earnings and valuations, earnings is the easier one. Valuations is the harder one. And valuations feel arbitrary in the beginning till you actually start cracking it. And how do you crack it? You start understanding what the consensus expectation around, or the consensus ability to pay something for a stock is. What is collective psychology telling me about how much a stock is currently valued and how much it’ll be valued? I always wanna know what expectations are. Is the price reflecting that expectation? How is it different from my expectation? And then reconcile all these things.”
On the danger of reading institutional reports
Financial content often misinterprets sell-side research because it treats institutional analysis as retail advice. Sagar warns against consuming reports that were never written for a general audience.
“These sell side reports are meant for the buy side, right? I see a lot of people giving shit to analysts saying, oh, these are too detailed, these are not relevant. But that’s not meant for you. Why are you reading something that is not meant for you and then criticising what is written there? I feel like this goes wrong horribly a lot of times, because they consider these to be recommendations meant for the general public when they’re not. These reports getting published and coming out in the open does not mean they were meant for you. These are things to be taken into a lot of context, which fund managers are able to consume.”
On using earnings to read the real economy
You do not need to be a stock picker to benefit from earnings calls. For professionals across all industries, quarterly results offer a grounded reality check against broader macroeconomic narratives.
“It sort of gives you a on ground reality check. You may have a situation where the macro numbers say one thing, the government is saying one thing in terms of what’s happening, but it’s not translating into on ground benefits. Connecting that aerial view to your ground view, this definitely helps as an exercise. We are talking about the 500 top companies in India. You are getting a sense of what the largest companies in India do and whether the macro is connecting down or not. And if you are in a certain industry, it definitely helps to know what is working, what is not working, and position yourself or develop your skillset a certain way.”
On fact-checking management claims
It is tempting to take confident management commentary at face value. However, Sagar suggests a simple framework for calling out bluff: cross-checking the numbers with peers, historical trends, and simple arithmetic.
“At the end of the day, what is being said, what is being done and the numbers that are delivered should be in line. If there is a mismatch in any of the three, as an investor, you’ll know. If the management has set that we will deliver 25% growth, and they deliver 15% in the first quarter, the ask rate for the next three quarters is much larger. You start looking at peers. Are peers talking the same language? Then how can this one company grow? You can evidence a lot of these using numbers and figure out whether what is happening is possible from a mathematical standpoint or not.”
On the importance of brevity in research
For anyone writing or consuming financial analysis, producing longer reports often feels like a proxy for deeper research. But true insight lies in the ability to distill complexity into a concise, actionable summary.
“Brevity is one thing because these run into pages and pages and pages, just making it concise and extracting what is important. You may write a hundred page report, but if you’re not able to tell me the crux of it in a line that is not more than 20 seconds, I’m not sold on this. So the one thing to probably avoid doing is chasing length, chasing a lot of fillers, and probably just sticking to an actionable or that one insight that you’re waiting for.”

Space is hard. It is a cliché that gets thrown around a lot, but its realities are difficult to grasp until you try to build hardware that operates in a vacuum, extreme radiation, and wild thermal cycles—all with zero tolerance for failure. For Earth observation companies, that hardware difficulty is compounded by a business reality: satellite imagery is essentially a data business waiting for its “GPS moment,” hampered by inconsistent supply due to cloud cover.
Suyash Singh, co-founder and CEO of GalaxEye, is attempting to solve this by building India’s first OptoSAR satellite—a system that combines optical cameras with synthetic aperture radar (SAR) to see through clouds and provide consistent, daily imagery. Pranav Agarwal sat down with Suyash to understand the journey from an IIT Madras Hyperloop team to building space tech.
The conversation covered the technical hurdles of synchronising optical and SAR sensors travelling at seven kilometres per second, the realities of miniaturising radars for drones as a frugal testing ground, and how the IN-SPACe reorganisation catalysed the Indian private space ecosystem. Suyash also broke down the economics of Earth observation and what it is like to book a launch slot with SpaceX.
Some of the things they said stuck with us. We’re sharing six of them here.
On the “GPS moment” for Earth observation
Most of us use GPS and satellite communication daily without a second thought, but satellite imaging hasn’t reached that level of commoditisation. Suyash explains that this is largely due to weather dependency—optical cameras can’t see through clouds.
“GPS is commoditised. Communication is done. And then we started digging a little more why it is not commoditised. And the possible reason that we could reach was that there’s no consistency in satellite imagery today. You may get an imagery today, tomorrow it must be cloudy. You can’t get an image. Third day you’ll get it. Again, fourth day you might not get it. Two months of monsoons, no imagery, and then three months later you’ll get one imagery. Will you rely on such kind of service level agreements? Answer is no.
It’s as good as imagine if GPS would have been dependent on weather. You can book your Uber today, but you can’t book your Uber tomorrow. And then Uber will tell you three months later that you can book it today or not. This is where observation stuck. There is no constant input of satellite imagery which is consistent and intuitive to the end user to build a SaaS application on top.”
On why space hardware is unforgiving
If a car breaks down, you take it to a service centre. If a drone fails, you land it and swap a part. Suyash highlights how the inability to repair assets combined with extreme environmental conditions makes space a uniquely brutal domain.
“Space is hard because you cannot get the asset back to repair. For example, you’re using an automotive car, and the gearbox was faultier. You’ll call all the automotive back to your service center, and you’ll change the gearbox and say, ‘Okay, great. Maintenance done. Bye-bye.’ So there’s a lot of allowance to fail on ground, even on drones. You can take it back, change a few things, do something, and there’s zero tolerance in space because you just can’t reach there. So the fact that it is hard is the number one point about that is you can can’t get it back to repair. Most of the things you can repair on Earth, right? But even if a satellite is repairable, you just can’t get it back.
So that is one thing that makes it super hard. Second point, which is much more of a technical explanation, is you have very limited power in space. I mean, you can’t take a transmission line and power plug onto your satellite and say, ‘Okay, I’m getting power from transmission lines.’ So you’re only dependent on sun, which means you’re only dependent on solar panels.”
On miniaturising before space
Space iteration is expensive. Startups in India don’t have the luxury of launching multiple failed satellites to perfect their sensors. GalaxEye’s approach was to miniaturise their radar and test it aggressively on drones and aircraft first.
“The kind of pricing that you’ll get from a foreign vendor to build SAR for you is something a startup can’t afford. So then you have to say, ‘Okay, can I build first a SAR, and then I’ll think about an OptoSAR?’ So the step one was for us to build a SAR, and that was also a moment of realisation that probably there are no SAR companies in the country. Should we put it together and then launch and then reiterate and understand? The answer is no, you’re based in India, you will not be able to find that kind of capital to iterate in space. You can’t send up and then learn from it and do it again and again. Maybe you will have one or two attempts. So we said, ‘Okay, it is better to maybe test out systems in a much more frugal manner.’
So what we did is we miniaturised the SAR and optical in such a way that we can put it on an aircraft or a drone or a HAPS. So for us, the first three years were all about testing whether my sensor really works in a limited environment.”
On integrating optical and SAR (OptoSAR)
Putting a camera and a radar on the same satellite isn’t just about bolting them together. Because they naturally look at the Earth from different angles, aligning them perfectly while travelling at orbital speeds is a profound engineering challenge.
“So if my satellite is above Bangalore, so probably I’m imaging Indore with optical camera, and you are imaging Dubai with SAR. When you put these two sensors by default, then you’re effectively imaging two different areas on space, which is not the objective. So what you really need to do is see and marry these sensors in such a way that they look at the same area, and they do same time imaging. So they have to look... otherwise, satellites move at seven kilometers per second. So when you start imaging and you are delayed by a second in camera or SAR, you’ve lost seven kilometers of concurrent imaging.”
On the realities of launching with SpaceX
SpaceX hasn’t just lowered the cost of launch; they’ve productised the entire experience. Suyash describes the process of booking a rocket ride, which is remarkably similar to buying a commercial flight ticket online.
“SpaceX has done a great job in making their launch slot visible to you on a website or an app, like a booking platform. For example, you’re booking an airplane ticket. You can pretty much book on SpaceX a similar way, you can book a launch. It’s as simple as that. The moment you book the launch, they then get in touch with you to get more information about your asset, your payload, legitimacy of your payload, et cetera. Then you get into a very simple agreement. And then there are payment milestones. So initially you’ll have to pay 10 to 30%, then 50%, 60%. And over the course of your engagement and agreement, you are allowed to pay in milestones.
So once that is done, then there is the exchange of information that, okay, here is how you’re going to attach the payload to the satellite. And then before a duration of the launch, they’re going to give you a guidance that this is the time when you need to reach there. It’s like your train is going to leave the station, so you will have to come at that particular point to hop onto that train.”
On the friction in selling satellite data
While the technology is advanced, the downstream market for satellite imagery remains challenging. Commercial customers don’t want raw pixels or complex analysis; they just want the final, actionable insight.
“I mean, if you are a commodity trader, and if I tell you, ‘Hey, here’s my data. Now you do your own analysis of where is shrimp, how much shrimp is available, how much copper is available, and whatnot,’ you’ll be like, ‘I don’t want to build a R&D team on top of this imagery analytics and do.’ So I think there is still a gap between data providers and insight generators. And that gap is quite big currently, and that causes discomfort to anyone to kind of come and try satellite imagery.
The SaaS companies who can actually build an application to do operations and maintenance of all the transmission lines, they’re not getting the right data at a consistent pace to build a solution for their end users. So imagine you’re a transmission company and I’m a SaaS company. If I promise you that I will give you one image, one report of maintenance where it needs to be done every week, and I didn’t get the images for three weeks because of clouds, then you’re gonna cancel the contract.”

Hi, I’m Kashish and a while ago, I did something slightly unhinged. I went through 144 concalls, across 18 microfinance companies, spanning eight quarters, just to watch a single credit cycle play out in slow motion. The idea was to see, in the actual words of the people running these businesses, how an entire industry lends its way into a crisis and then claws its way back out.
The Chatter by Zerodha
Has the microfinance credit cycle turned?
Hi, I’m Kashish and I work on Plotlines…
Read more
6 months ago · 42 likes · 13 comments · Zerodha
But research has a way of leaving you with more questions than you started with. By the end, I understood what had happened to microfinance. I was much less sure I understood why it keeps happening, over and over, roughly every few years, like clockwork.
So I called someone who’s been watching Indian banking for longer than I’ve been alive. Tamal Bandyopadhyay has covered this beat for close to three decades. When I first spoke to him, he refused to call himself an expert. He prefers “observer.” But this is a man who was earlier associated with Bandhan Bank, is currently a senior advisor at Jana Small Finance Bank, and whose book Pandemonium is the reason I started reading about Indian banks in the first place. So “observer” is doing a lot of heavy lifting.
Here’s what I took away.
What even is a microfinance loan?
I opened with a surprisingly hard question: what actually counts as microfinance? Almost anything can be dressed up as one. A joint-liability group loan is microfinance. A small unsecured loan from a fintech app looks like microfinance. An unsecured loan to a kirana shop could be microfinance. So when Kotak and a small finance bank like AU both report a “microfinance book,” are they even describing the same thing?
For the longest time, they weren’t. Until April 2022, there was no clean definition at all.
“It was not exactly defined what is microfinance, which is why there were a lot of overlapping between microfinance entities and the banks.”
Everyone was doing the same thing, nobody owned the turf, and that ambiguity is exactly where the over-leveraging crept in.
What the RBI did in 2022 was quietly clever. It stopped defining microfinance by who was lending and started defining it by what the loan was.
“If you’re a bank, the rules are same for you. If you are a non-bank, the rules are same for you.”
The dividing line is now household income. Lend to a household earning up to ₹3 lakh a year, within the repayment limits, and it’s microfinance, full stop. There was one detail that stuck with me though: the share of secured loans an MFI is allowed to hold has been quietly raised over the years, from 15% to 25% to 40%. Why? Tamal didn’t dress it up.
“This is to save the microfinance entity.”
The regulator is handing these lenders more room to lean on safer collateral, because it has watched them fall into trouble too many times.
A business built to break every few years
Microfinance blows up unusually often, and the blowups tend to hit the whole industry rather than one bad company. So I asked him: is fragility just a feature of this business?
His answer was that you’re lending to the most vulnerable slice of the economy, and vulnerability comes at you from every direction at once. Microfinance is, at heart, a replacement for the village moneylender, and that’s the whole moral case for the interest rates.
“Even though we are charging 24%, 26%, 28% odd, still we are much less than money lender.”
But that borrower base is exposed to shocks a secured-lending bank never faces. Floods, cyclones, earthquakes, all regional, all capable of wiping out repayment across a district. Then there’s politics. Ahead of elections, state governments float loan-waiver promises, and even when those promises legally don’t apply to RBI-regulated lenders, the damage is done to the borrower’s mindset.
“Even if I’m able to pay, I’ll say I’ll not pay because the state government is there to help me out.”
One person defaulting because they can’t is a credit event. A whole village refusing to pay because they think they won’t have to is a broken culture. And culture, once broken, is very hard to rebuild.
The most striking thing he said was about how investors have simply made peace with all this. They price the boom-bust rhythm in from the start. The smart money, he said, goes in knowing that “every four or five years, I’ll not get any money for two years or three years.” So in the good years they refuse to compromise on returns, because they’re already banking against the bad years they know are coming. The cyclicality isn’t a bug the market is trying to fix. It’s a feature the market has learned to underwrite.
I wanted to know if the regional exposure could ever be engineered away. His answer was blunt: no. To make the point, he walked through what the latest downturn did to the five biggest microfinance states by borrower count.
Same shock, very different outcomes. Tamil Nadu barely moved; the others were gutted. The difference, he said, comes down to how leveraged the borrowers were and how the lenders behaved. “It all depends on the lenders.”
The kids at the bar
This was my favourite part of the conversation, because instead of a statistic, Tamal told me a story.
He was in a bar in Kolkata he used to frequent in his university days. A table of five or six young men, early twenties, were making more noise than everyone else. He got curious and struck up a conversation.
“They all had taken loan from fintech to finance their beer drinking.”
Some were giving tuitions, a couple came from comfortable families, a lawyer’s son, a businessman’s son. And they were paying 44% interest. So why take it? Two reasons, both revealing. One, no bank would touch them. And two, they’d been sold a story:
“This is the way I will get you into the credit cycle. Credit bureau will catch you, and later you’ll be credit-worthy.”
Here’s why this matters for the whole industry. A microfinance lender checks the credit bureau, sees a borrower already has two loans, and lends a third because the rules allow up to three. What it cannot see is that the same person has two or three more loans sitting with fintechs and loan apps, at 40% or 50%, none of it reliably showing up in bureau data. The lender thinks it’s the third creditor. It’s actually the sixth.
I asked whether these fintechs were operating illegally. He was careful, and I respect that he didn’t overreach.
“Not exactly like that, but they’re not caught.”
What he would say is that the RBI is clearly worried, is tightening the screws on digital lending, and is moving towards a regime where these players need explicit approval.
The red-letter day
If you want to understand the most recent crisis specifically, Tamal traces it to one decision.
In 2022, the RBI freed lenders to set their own interest rates. Earlier, rates were capped as a function of borrowing cost; now the market would decide, and the regulator assumed competition would push rates down . Tamal wrote a column at the time calling it a red-letter day for the industry. I asked if he stood by it. He did, but not the way he’d hoped.
“I’m sure industry would hate me for this. It’s been misused.”
He noted that even the RBI’s own Deputy Governor, Swaminathan, had publicly flagged that lenders weren’t being judicious with the freedom they’d been handed.
That freedom also quietly killed the industry’s foundational model. The joint-liability group, or JLG, works by lending to a group of women at a single common rate, with the group collectively guaranteeing each loan. But once you can price each borrower differently, the model falls apart.
“How do you create a group where you are lending money at different rates to different persons? Certainly it will not work.”
Digitisation finished the job. The old ritual of weekly village meetings and a group leader collecting on everyone’s behalf is gone. It cut operating costs, but it also severed the human contact that made the group model work in the first place.
This one was self-inflicted
Every earlier crisis had an external villain. A flood. An election. One rogue lender in Assam or Andhra Pradesh. This time, I put it to him that the villain was the industry itself. He agreed, and didn’t flinch.
“This is actually made by probably the entire industry, barring exceptions.”
The scale of the boom, and the reckoning that followed.
A fourfold expansion during the bullish phase, then a violent contraction. He mentioned coming across a single borrower carrying fourteen separate loans. Every guardrail, the income cap, the three-loan limit, was simply overrun.
And crucially, this was never a demand story.
“You give the borrowers more money, push down their throat, which they are not able to pay back.”
It was, in his words, “a completely supply side problem. You can’t blame the borrowers.” He reached for a sharper word too, calling it “harakiri,” a collective suicide by an industry that assumed the good times would never end. Then the banks pulled the plug.
“The main source of money, the banking sector, they have closed the tap.”
For all but the largest players, bank funding has dried up, balance sheets are shrinking, and the smaller lenders are running out of road.
The striptease test
My last question was the selfish one. As an investor trying to play this cycle, what do I actually look for, given that NPAs only tell you about the disaster after it’s happened?
His answer was a single word: underwriting. And then came the best analogy of the conversation. He took me back to Raghuram Rajan’s clean-up of the banking system, when banks were hiding the true state of their books. Rajan’s message, as Tamal told it, was that his auditors would go into every room of the house and find what was hidden.
“Bankers were doing belly dancing. And Raghuram Rajan forced them to do striptease. So essentially, they were stark naked.”
Two banks turned out to be carrying 30%-plus bad loans. Today, after they rebuilt their risk management, the system’s net NPA sits below 1%.
The lesson transfers directly. Unsecured lending is cash-flow based, so the entire game is the quality of underwriting and the discipline to say no to over-leveraging. The economics can absolutely work; the margins are high enough to absorb real credit costs. But only if the lender resists the temptation to shove loans out the door when times are good. As an investor, that discipline is the thing to hunt for, long before it ever shows up in the NPA line.
So, what comes next?
Tamal’s read on where the industry goes is unsentimental. Many mid-sized MFIs are quietly turning into business correspondents, originating and collecting loans on behalf of banks rather than carrying the risk themselves. The smallest are simply shutting shop. The largest can hold on, for now, but even they are living on borrowed time.
“It’s high time they need to reinvent themselves. It can’t go on.”
The good news, and he was clear about this, is that the worst of this cycle is behind us. The bad news is that if the industry has taught us anything across Andhra, Assam, and now this self-inflicted one, it’s that “behind us” always comes with an expiry date.
This is just the skeleton of a much richer conversation. Tamal was extraordinarily generous with his time, and we covered far more ground, and far more stories, than fit on a page. If you’d rather hear it in his own words, the full conversation is up now on YouTube , Apple Podcast & Spotify .

Unsung Science, The Man Who Invented QR codes ( link )
Last week in the reading edition, I mentioned I was listening to the Intermission episode on Bajaj Finance. I finally finished it after a long time, and it’s genuinely good — not just about the business, but about the people behind it, how obsessive and meticulous they were. It left me thinking that in most companies, the people are the business model, not the other way round. But that’s a separate thought.
Coming to the topic: in that podcast, Rohin mentioned that QR codes were invented by a man named Masahiro Hara. I looked him up and found a podcast episode where he tells the story himself, and it’s a great listen.
A few things stood out. First, QR codes are barely thirty years old, which is hard to believe given how much we depend on them today — you couldn’t get from point A to B in most Indian cities anymore without one. Hara worked at Denso, a car-parts subsidiary of Toyota, and the idea came to him during a lunch break in 1993, while he was playing Go, the Chinese board game. The two-dimensional grid of black and white stones on the board was the spark — he realised a barcode didn’t have to be a single line of stripes, it could be a grid.
The problem with regular barcodes was that they were one-dimensional: scratch them, tilt the scanner at the wrong angle, and they wouldn’t read. A two-dimensional code fixed that — it could be read from any angle, at any distance, and would still work even if a third of it was damaged or covered.
It took about twenty years for QR codes to catch on in India, with Paytm leading the charge around 2015-16 pushing QR payments at scale. And in the decade since, it’s become the backbone of how the country pays for things.
Worth a listen if you want to hear Hara describe the whole arc himself — including how his bosses weren’t impressed for the first six years.
What is Kashish watching?
Gobardhan, SATAT, and the economics of compressed biogas ( link )
I stumbled upon this video while trying to understand the Gobardhan scheme, mostly because I was confused about how it differed from the SATAT scheme, which we had covered earlier .
It turns out the two aren’t really competing schemes. Gobardhan has increasingly become the umbrella under which India’s compressed biogas (CBG) ecosystem is being built, while SATAT is one of the mechanisms that creates demand for that gas.
That led me down a rabbit hole on the economics of the industry, and I found the underlying problems much more interesting than the policy itself.
The biggest one is geography. Biogas plants have to be located close to feedstock—crop residue, cattle waste, municipal waste, and so on—because transporting raw waste over long distances simply doesn’t make economic sense. But the demand for gas is concentrated in cities. Bridging that gap isn’t easy. Either you inject the gas into a pipeline network, which many plants don’t have access to, or you transport it in cylinders, which creates another logistics problem altogether.
Then there’s the question of pricing.
Compressed biogas is generally more expensive than conventional natural gas, which means city gas distributors and oil marketing companies have little incentive to buy it purely on economics. It becomes attractive only when fossil fuel prices spike or because blending mandates require them to procure it. That’s an important reminder that not every clean-energy technology succeeds because it’s the cheapest option from day one.
Finally, unlike many commodities, CBG doesn’t lend itself to a neat national price. A plant connected to a gas pipeline has very different economics from one trucking cylinders hundreds of kilometres away. Feedstock differs. Logistics differ. End markets differ. The economics are intensely local.
The video itself is fairly introductory, but it sent me down an interesting line of thinking. Sometimes the hardest part of the energy transition isn’t building the technology but figuring out the logistics and market design that make the technology economically viable. And compressed biogas is a great example of that.
