Japan’s policy rate is at its highest in 31 years .
And theoretically, that should make the currency — the yen — stronger. Higher rates are supposed to attract investors into the country.
Instead, the yen has fallen to its weakest level since 1986. That’s 40 years .
Higher yields. Weaker currency. At the same time.
I’m not getting into the dynamics driving Japan’s economy right now. But what I want to tell you is about something called a Carry Trade that depends entirely on what happens to Japan’s interest rates and currency. It’s a not-so-secret trade that has funded a huge chunk of the world’s financial system for the better part of three decades.
Let’s take it from the top.
Imagine you could borrow money for almost nothing, and immediately lend it out or invest it somewhere else for a much higher rate. You’d do it all day, right? That’s a carry trade. Simple.
Borrow in a currency where interest rates are low. Convert it into a currency where rates are high. Park it there and pocket the difference — the “carry.”
If the exchange rate doesn’t move against you, you’ve made a spread for doing almost nothing.
I’ll explain.
Let’s take a simplified dollar-yen situation for the carry trade and assume you borrow ¥10,000 (Japanese yen) instead of dollars, because Japan barely charges any interest.
Exchange rate today: ¥100 = $1
So you borrow ¥10,000 = $100
You take that $100 and put it in a US account paying 5% interest.
A year later,
Your $100 has grown to $105 (thanks, 5%)
But maybe you owe just ¥10,050 on the yen loan because Japan’s rate was close to 0%.
But you still have to convert the money to collect your profit.
Scenario A: Exchange rate stays the same (¥100 = $1)
Your $105 converts back to ¥10,500
You pay back the ¥10,050 you owe
You keep ¥450 profit, for doing basically nothing.
That’s the carry trade working as intended. But here’s where currency movement matters.
Scenario B: The yen gets stronger (now ¥90 = $1)
Your $105 converts back to only ¥9,450 (because each dollar now buys fewer yen)
But you still owe ¥10,050
You’re ¥600 short. You lost money, even though your US investment paid you 5%.
You just lost money on a trade that “should” have been free money. So it’s not really an arbitrage trade here because it comes with currency risk.
But anyway, now that you understand how that works, let’s get back to Japan’s role in this now. Because for nearly three decades, the currency everyone borrowed was the yen.
And there’s a reason for that.
You see, after Japan’s asset bubble burst in the early 1990s, the country spent the next 30 years fighting deflation. The Bank of Japan’s answer was to hold interest rates at, or below, zero for almost the entire period. Meanwhile, economies like the US kept raising and lowering rates through normal cycles, often landing well above zero.
That gap — near 0% in Japan, 3-5%+ almost everywhere else — turned the yen into the world’s default funding currency.
Hedge funds, pension funds, insurers, and Japan’s own army of retail investors — collectively nicknamed Mrs Watanabe — all did some version of the same trade: borrow cheap yen, buy US Treasuries, American tech stocks, Indian equities, emerging-market bonds, anything that paid more than zero.
Estimates of how big this trade got vary wildly, because so much of it happens off balance sheet through derivatives, but figures of $1-2 trillion in exposure get thrown around by analysts trying to size it (Japanese investors now hold $12 trillion in foreign assets so you’d assume a good subset of that it thanks to the carry trade), .
And this is why the yen carry trade matters so much more than a typical currency story. It isn’t really about Japan. The money from this trade has played a role in global asset prices — US tech stocks included.
What happens when it breaks?
Well, the trade only works if the yen stays weak and it is cheap to borrow. The moment the yen starts rising, the math flips. The yen debt costs more to repay, and if you’re leveraged, that can wipe out years of carry-trade gains in days. So you rush to sell your foreign assets, convert back into yen, and repay the loan — which pushes the yen up even further, which forces the next trader to do the same thing.
And this played out in August 2024.
The Bank of Japan had raised rates — barely, from near-zero to 0.25% — a few days earlier. Then a weak US jobs report landed on August 2 and revived recession fears, raising bets that the Fed would start cutting interest rates. The rate gap that had powered the trade suddenly looked like it was closing from both ends.
Leveraged yen shorts scrambled to cover. The yen jumped roughly 6% in about a week. The Nikkei 225 crashed 12.4% in a single session. Sentiment took a beating.
Even the Indian markets crashed due to the ripple effect this event had on the world even though the FII yen exposure was on the lower end. Sentiment.
That’s the risk that is sitting inside a trade that usually is quite boring.
Which brings us to today
Since that crash, the Bank of Japan hasn’t stopped normalising interest rates. And they’ve steadily inched higher and higher to their highest since 1995.
Now under the old logic from what happened in 2024, that should be squeezing the carry trade to death. Rising Japanese yields make it more expensive and discourages new carry positions even without a dramatic crash.
And money should be coming back into the country and supporting the yen. Yet the yen just hit a 40-year low anyway.
What gives?
Well, there could be a couple of reasons why the “higher yields should mean a stronger yen” story isn’t playing out. Yet.
For starters, the gap remains.
See, inflation is running hot in the US too. It’s well above the 2% target the central bank has. And reading between the lines of what the Fed is doing, there’s a possibility that they might choose to hike interest rates.
Meanwhile, there’s something I didn’t tell you. Sure, Japan’s benchmark policy rate is at a thirty-year high. But that high is 1%.
Yup, just 1%.
So, the spread between Japan and the US still remains quite significant and could even get wider if the predictions on what the Fed will do plays out.
Which means, the carry trade hasn’t lost its reason to exist.
The second reason is that some of Japan’s rising bond yields aren’t actually a vote of confidence in the country.
The current government has quite the expansionary fiscal policy. Which means more spending and higher debt levels. Markets have started pricing in a bigger risk premium on Japan’s long-dated debt as a result.
When yields rise because a central bank is tightening to fight inflation, it usually pulls a currency up with it. When yields rise because bond investors are demanding more compensation for a government’s spending plans, it can do the opposite — it signals rising fiscal risk, and currencies don’t reward that.
So, what does all this mean for the carry trade? Will we see a repeat of 2024? Or will the hawkish US Fed cancel it out?
Honestly, both camps have a case right now.
One camp says the fundamentals that kept the yen cheap for a decade are quietly eroding thanks to a more confident Bank of Japan, rising Japanese wages, and higher bond yields. Hence, capital will keep drifting back toward Japan over time. Some fund managers say they already see this happening as money starts flowing back into Japan.
The other camp believes that even though the yield gap has narrowed, there is still real money to be made. Especially given that there’s broadly a stance within the BOJ that near-term interest rate hikes will be limited. And speculators are more than happy to take bets against the yen too. They believe it will continue to fall (which helps the carry trade). And hence, these bets have now reached a 9-year high . In fact, analysts at JPMorgan say that “the BOJ’s potential rate hike and FX support are already substantially priced in by the market at this point, whereas both moves were surprises two years ago.”
For now, it looks like real money is finding its way back to a trade that’s paid out for thirty years. But it may not take much for the tide to turn as well.

Let me tell you about a man who sparked one of the biggest investment revolutions of the last 50 years. This revolution wasn't about earning higher returns; it was about saving on costs.
Costs—like management fees—are a tiny percentage charged to manage your investments. How can saving on something so small be revolutionary?
Hold that thought for a moment.
We all love the power of compounding. At 15% annual returns, your money doubles roughly every 5 years:
The first doubling added Rs 1 lakh to your wealth. The last doubling? Rs 33 lakh. That is the power of compounding.
But few talk about how costs compound the exact same way. Costs are like termites, silently eating into your wealth for years before you even notice.
The man who understood this was John C. Bogle, the founder of Vanguard, one of the largest asset management companies in the United States.
In 1976, he launched the first index fund for individual investors. Instead of picking stocks or timing the market, index funds—like the ICICI Pru Nifty 50 Index Fund—simply buy and hold an entire index. No star fund managers, no massive research teams, and consequently, much lower fees.
Wall Street laughed at this launch. They called it “Bogle’s Folly.”
Why would anyone settle for average market returns when you could pay a professional to beat the market?
But Bogle’s argument was that an actively managed fund tries to beat the market, but charges higher fees. An index fund just delivers the market return but at almost no cost. If the higher fees eat up the outperformance, the investor ends up with the same amount, or less. So why pay for it?
I am not here to settle the active-versus-passive debate. I am here to talk about costs. And Bogle is where that story begins.
What did Bogle achieve? A Bloomberg analyst estimated he saved investors $500 billion in fees. Furthermore, Vanguard’s low-cost model forced competitors to cut fees, pushing total savings to roughly $1 trillion (₹95 lakh crore, imagine giving ₹95,000 each to 100 crore people).
So here is the question: do you know what your costs are?
The Indian version of the fight
Bogle, even as a student at Princeton in 1951, was against the layers of intermediary costs in the fund industry.
In India, we got our own version of this fight in January 2013. Mutual funds charge you an expense ratio, primarily the annual fee for managing your money.
Before 2013, this included everything: the fund manager’s fee, operational costs, and the commission paid to the distributor who sold you the fund. You had no way of knowing how much was going where.
Then SEBI said every fund must offer a Direct plan, one without the distributor’s commission.
So now, someone buying through a distributor (the Regular plan) pays an expense ratio that includes the commission. Someone buying directly pays the one without it. Same fund, same stocks, same manager.
We looked at 21 large-cap fund pairs running continuously from 2013 over 13.5 years. Regular plans typically charged 2.09% versus Direct plans’ 1.10%. That ~1% difference sounds small, but it’s n ot.
Here is what that 1% actually costs you on a Rs 10,000 monthly SIP, using the typical returns from these 21 funds:
In 10 years, commissions have eaten 4% of your wealth. In 20 years, nearly 10%. In 30 years, over 15%.
The return you lose in year 5 never compounds in year 6, or year 7, or year 25. Bogle called this “the tyranny of compounding costs.” Costs do not just subtract from your returns. They subtract from the future compounding of those returns.
What you should do : If you are working with a mutual fund distributor who genuinely helps you choose funds based on your goals, does the research, and keeps you disciplined, then you know what you are paying for, and it may well be worth it. But if you are in a ‘Regular’ plan without receiving any real advice, that 1% is just a distribution cost sitting inside your expense ratio. The expense ratio for both plans is disclosed in every fund’s factsheet; make sure to check what you are paying for.
What active management really costs
Multiple academic studies over decades have shown that most actively managed funds, after fees, fail to consistently beat the market. The research existed long before Bogle. But he was the first to act on it, building an index fund in 1976 for small investors, when the technology to track stocks, handle dividends, and corporate actions daily at scale barely existed.
We compared expense ratios across 18 fund houses in India where both an active large-cap fund and a passive Nifty 50 ETF exist. The typical ETF charges 0.07% and a typical active fund charges 1.04%, 15 times the cost of an ETF.
There are also index mutual funds in between, which are passive like ETFs but do not require a demat account. The typical Nifty 50 index fund charges about 0.26%.
That gap of about 1% between active funds and ETFs is the extra cost you pay for a fund manager to pick stocks. Your fund manager must beat the index by at least 1% every year just to break even on costs. If they do not, the gap compounds. Here is what that looks like on a Rs 10,000 monthly SIP:
Have Indian fund managers justified this cost?
Over 13.5 years, most large-cap active funds delivered higher returns than the typical Nifty 50 ETF. But over shorter periods, the results are less convincing. Over any given 5-year stretch, only about 2 out of 3 active funds beat the index. Over 7-year stretches, about 3 out of 4. We would never know which side we will fall. Globally, however, passive is winning
Note: Picking a good active fund requires a lot of homework on understanding the manager and their strategy. We covered how to evaluate active funds here on Varsity . If you are not doing that kind of analysis, it is worth asking: why not stick to a low-cost passive fund?
A few things about the expense ratios
The mutual fund returns and the net asset values (NAV) you see are always after deducting the expense ratio.
Starting April 2026, SEBI also changed how the cost (TER: Total Expense Ratio) is disclosed.
TER = Base Expense ratio (BER includes management fee, operating costs, etc.) + brokerage + transaction costs + statutory charges.
SEBI also caps what funds can charge, and the cap depends on the fund’s size.
See, the cost of managing and researching stocks is roughly the same whether 1,000 people invest or 1,00,000 people invest. So, as a fund grows, SEBI requires it to charge lower fees. For equity funds, the BER cap starts at 2.10% for funds up to Rs 500 crore; while the fund you invested in has a total size of more than Rs 50,000 crore, the BER cap drops to 0.95%.
When comparing funds, first look at the BER number, not TER, because transaction costs vary month to month, but BER is what you consistently pay. If two funds have similar BERs but one has a higher TER, it probably signals that one fund is buying and selling more.
Bogle wrote about costs in a college thesis in 1951. He built a company around it in 1975. Wall Street mocked him with “Bogle’s Folly.” Today, his followers call themselves Bogleheads, and they are everywhere, from the US to India.
Every rupee that goes to fees is a rupee that stops compounding in your favor.
Seventy-five years and halfway across the world, fund houses across the world are competing on price, and expense ratios are coming down. What Bogle did was nothing short of revolutionary.

Most market data tells you what a price did. One number tells you what people did with the price.
Every evening after the market closes, the exchanges publish a file most investors have never opened. It is a plain spreadsheet, one row per stock, and among the familiar columns of open, high, low, and close sits the delivery percentage, a figure almost nobody looks at. It is free and public, and it shows something a price chart cannot.
For a few weeks now, that number has been behaving unusually in one corner of the market. Before we get to which, it helps to understand what it is, because the whole signal rests on it.
What the Number Actually Measures
Every trade ends either as an intraday position or an overnight one. Intraday is when the buyer squares off before the close, taking a profit or a loss without ever meaning to hold overnight. An overnight position is when the trader lets it settle, taking actual delivery of the shares into their demat account.
Delivery percentage measures the second group: the share of the day’s traded volume that was delivered rather than squared off. A high reading means an unusually large proportion of participants chose to hold. A low reading means most of the activity was intraday churn, opened and closed before the bell.
One detail makes it meaningful. It is netted, so a trader who buys and sells the same stock within the day cancels out, and only the net position carried into settlement counts as delivery. A high reading is therefore not noise; it means shares were carried through to settlement instead of being squared off intraday. Both exchanges publish it free at the end of each day, the NSE in its daily bhavcopy and the BSE in its gross deliverables report, calculated the same way on each, delivered quantity divided by total traded quantity.
What It Tells You About a Single Stock
On its own, one high-delivery day means little; any single session can be an outlier. The signal appears if we stop looking at a single day and look at one stock over time. Ranking every session’s delivery against that stock’s own history, a pattern emerges. Most days sit in an ordinary middle band, a few sit far above it, and when those high days start clustering, especially at particular price levels, they suggest something more deliberate than ordinary trading.
The key is to judge a stock against itself. A reading of 45 percent might be extraordinary for one stock and ordinary for another, since stocks differ in ownership, float, and a stock’s normal range of delivery percentage. Comparing a stock to its own record, not to the market, is what turns a raw number into a signal.
Here is one stock read exactly that way, Cochin Shipyard, chosen only to show the method.
The shaded band is the stock’s ordinary range of delivery. The marked sessions are the days it pushed well above that range, when an unusually large share of volume settled into accounts rather than being squared off. Set against the price panel below, they show where in the price the holding happened. That is the whole method: not the level of delivery on any given day, but how far it sits above normal for that stock, and where it clusters.
From One Stock to a Sector
Most people look at delivery data in isolation, often for a single stock. Things get more interesting when we look at an entire sector instead. For example, rather than looking at only IRCTC, we look at the delivery data across the whole railway sector.
If the entire sector shows similar behaviour at the same time, it tells us something is moving through that sector, not just one company.
A sector moving together is a louder signal, but a harder one to read. It might mean investors are deliberately buying across the group. It might also just be money flowing into an index or a theme, or holders sitting on their positions instead of selling. Delivery data tells us shares are being held. It does not tell us why.
This Week, the Signal Is in Railways
The railway stocks have lit up together.
Each row in the chart is one railway stock. The strip runs left to right across the last several months, with one thin line for every trading day. The colour of each line tells you how high delivery was that day, judged against that stock’s own history: a dark red line is a high-delivery day, and a pale, muted red line is a low-delivery day. The part to look at is the right end of each row, the most recent sessions. There, the lines turn dark red across all four stocks at once, which means every one of them is seeing high delivery at the same time.
The numbers beside each row make it concrete. IRCTC’s latest delivery percentage reading sits at the 99th percentile of its own record, with 63 percent of the day’s volume settled. RAILTEL is at the 96th percentile, BEML at the 95th, and IRFC at the 92nd. All four sit near the very top of their own historical delivery ranges.
That consistency is what makes the pattern worth noticing. This is not one stock posting an isolated spike. It is several related names simultaneously settling an unusually large share of their trading volume into delivery.
A Sector Sitting Near Its Lows
What makes the pattern worth a second look is where the prices are while it happens.
These are not stocks running to new highs on excitement. Across the sector, the prices have spent the year falling. The basket is down roughly 10 to 37 percent year to date, with Rail Vikas Nigam the weakest at about 37 percent and RITES the most resilient at about 10 percent, and most of the group trading near the low end of its yearly range.
The sector ran strong over the past couple of years and has since given much of it back. So two observations sit on top of each other: the prices near the bottom of their range, the holding near the top of its own. Shares are being settled into accounts on exactly the sessions when the stocks look weakest on a price chart. That is the shape that shows up when a beaten-down group is being quietly bought and held, while the price gives little sign of it.
What the Data Does and Does Not Say
This is the part that is easy to get wrong, so it is worth being careful.
When a large share of a group’s volume settles into accounts while prices sit near their lows, it is fair to call it accumulation. Investors are taking delivery, choosing to own the shares at these levels rather than trade them. The word fits.
What it does not carry is any claim about the bottom. Accumulation does not mean a stock has stopped falling or that the price is about to turn. It means only that some investors are willing to buy and hold at these prices, which is a statement about them, not about the price. They can be early, and they can be wrong. A stock can be accumulated the whole way down, delivery high at every step, while the price keeps sliding. Willingness to buy at a level does not make it a floor.
There is one more reason for caution, a technical one. Not every share that shows up as delivery was bought to be held. Take BTST, buy today and sell tomorrow: the buyer still takes delivery today, because the shares are credited before they are sold, so on the day of purchase that trade is indistinguishable from genuine accumulation and counts fully toward delivery, even though it will be gone within a day. A single large block deal can distort a session the same way. Ranking a stock against its own history dampens this noise, but it does not remove it.
So the value of this number is not that it predicts. It is that it tells you where to look. This week it is pointing at the railways, while the sector sits near its lows. It tells you investors are willing to take delivery at these prices. Whether those investors are ultimately right is something only time and price can answer.
The Closing Bell
One last thing about this number, because it helps to know where it comes from.
Your broker shows you price and volume: what a stock traded at, and how many shares changed hands. The delivery percentage is not something your broker produces. It comes from the exchanges, and from the clearing corporations that sit behind them, NSE Clearing for the NSE and BSE Clearing Limited for the BSE. These are the bodies that settle trades.
Settling a trade just means making sure it is completed. When someone buys a share, someone else has to actually hand it over. After every trading day, the clearing corporation works out who is owed shares and who has to deliver them, then moves those shares from one demat account to another through the depositories, NSDL and CDSL. It is the machinery that makes sure no trade is left half done.
The delivery percentage falls straight out of that process. It is not a guess or an opinion about a stock. It is simply a count of how many shares actually ended up in someone’s account, instead of being traded in and out the same day.
That is why it is worth watching. Price and volume tell you how busy a stock was. Delivery tells you how much of that activity was real ownership changing hands. This week, that number was pointing at the railways.

Gold and silver have never been just investments for us. We get them from our grandparents, we buy them for weddings and festivals, and there is an emotional weight to these metals that no other asset class carries.
But things are also changing. More people are recognizing the importance of precious metals as investments, mainly for diversification. In this newsletter, I want to walk you through the different ways you can invest in gold and silver in India today.
But first, a quick look at where prices have been recently.
Gold (24 karat) touched an all-time high of around ₹1,69,349 per 10 grams in early March 2026. Since then, it has pulled back to around ₹1,44,000 to ₹1,43,000 per 10 grams as of July 2026 so far. Still well above where it was a year ago, but off the peak.
MCX gold futures prices, January–July 2026. Prices in ₹ per 10 grams. Source: TradingView.
Silver is around ₹2,22,000 per kilogram right now, down sharply from its late-January peak of nearly ₹4 lakh. Silver has a dual identity that gold does not: it is both a precious metal and an industrial commodity. Solar panels, electric vehicles, electronics, and electrical grids all need silver.
MCX silver futures prices, January–July 2026. Prices in ₹ per kilogram. Source: TradingView.
With that context, let us get into the seven routes available to you.
1. Physical gold and silver
I am not talking about jewellery here. From a pure investment perspective, coins and bars are usually the more suitable options in physical form. Keep in mind that while coins and bars also carry small making (or minting) charges, they are significantly lower than jewelry.
There are two ways to buy physical gold and silver.
The first is the traditional way. You buy a coin or bar from a reputable jeweler or a trusted gold and silver seller. For gold, look for 24-karat coins or bars of 999 fineness. For silver investment, 999-fineness bars and coins are the industry standard.
The second way has become very common now. You buy through e-commerce platforms like Myntra, Flipkart, and others. You order online and the product gets delivered to you. This works for both gold and silver coins and bars.
Whichever way you go, there are a few things you should keep in mind.
Choose a trusted seller: Go with reputed and branded products. On digital platforms, this is especially important because you cannot inspect the product before it arrives.
Check the purity details: You can verify the purity of any gold or silver product by walking into most jewellery shops. They use XRF analyzers (a device to check the purity of metal) that can check the metal content without removing tamper-proof packaging.
Record the unboxing: This sounds like a small thing, but a short, continuous video while opening the parcel can really help if the package is damaged or the item is missing.
Compare the price: Check the price on the platform against the day’s IBJA or MCX rate. That way, you know how much extra you are paying over the prevailing metal price.
Pros: You hold the physical metal. Tangible ownership. Full control.
Cons: Storage is your responsibility (locker charges, insurance, security). When buying online, extra care is needed for authenticity. Resale involves purity checks and usually a small discount to spot.
2. Digital gold
You have probably seen this on your payment apps. You can buy gold starting from as little as ₹10 via UPI. The platform’s partner stores physical gold in vaults on your behalf. You can sell back at the platform’s sell price, or get the gold delivered to you physically.
I am going to keep this brief because there is one fundamental issue: digital gold is not regulated by SEBI, RBI, or any financial regulator. SEBI also cautioned investors about this.
The cost is higher than it looks. Digital platforms charge you more when you buy and pay you less when you sell (a 2% to 4% gap) compared to market prices. Plus, you lose 3% to government GST on every purchase.
We advise against investing in unregulated products.
Pros: Easy to access. Very low minimum investment.
Cons: Not regulated. Higher cost due to the buy-sell spread and GST. Platform-dependent safety.
3. Gold and silver ETFs
Now we look at the regulated stock market space. A gold or silver ETF is a fund that trades on the stock market, just like a company’s shares. You buy and sell these during market hours through your stockbroker using a standard demat account.
A common mistake is thinking a lower ETF price means a “cheaper” deal. It does not.
Think of ETFs like different-sized packets of chocolate. One brand sells a 10-gram packet, while another sells a 50-gram packet.
For example, GOLDCASE’s (Zerodha Gold ETF) structure works out to roughly 0.0016 gram of gold per unit, while one unit of Nippon India ETF Gold BeES corresponds to roughly 0.01 gram. So Gold BeES will naturally have a higher unit price even though both ETFs track the same underlying asset.
Each unit is backed by physical metal in secure vaults, regulated by SEBI. The fund house handles custody, insurance, and auditing.
Liquidity matters here. If an ETF does not have enough buyers and sellers, you might end up paying more than the metal is actually worth or selling for less. The way to check if you are buying or selling closer to market price is to look at the iNAV (Indicative Net Asset Value) of the scheme. It tells you what the underlying metal is actually worth at that moment.
Fund houses publish the iNAV throughout the trading day. Compare the market price with the iNAV, and you will know if you are getting a fair deal. Here is an example of how the iNAV page looks .
If you want a detailed guide on how to select an ETF, things like tracking error, expense ratios, and all of that, I have covered it in a separate piece .
Pros: SEBI regulated. Transparent pricing. Buy and sell during market hours. Low expense ratios. No storage headaches. Available for both gold and silver.
Cons: Need a demat and trading account. Liquidity can be an issue for smaller ETFs, always check iNAV. Cannot take physical delivery. Brokerage charges apply.
4. Gold and silver FoFs (Fund of Funds)
When people say “gold mutual fund” or “silver mutual fund,” this is what they mean. A FoF. Fund of Funds. A fund that invests in another fund.
When you invest in Gold and silver FoFs, the fund manager takes the money and invests in gold or silver ETFs, which are backed by the physical metal.
The big advantage: you do not need a demat account. You can invest through any mutual fund platform. You can set up a SIP starting from ₹100. Everything works like any other mutual fund.
But there is something you need to understand about how this actually works.
Mostly, when FoFs buy units of the underlying gold/silver ETFs, they invest at whatever price the ETF is trading at. So if the ETF is trading at a premium to the actual gold price, your FoF buys at that premium. If the ETF is at a discount, the FoF buys at that discount. Whatever pricing issues the ETF has, the FoF inherits them.
Say the gold price is ₹14,461 per gram. The gold ETF is trading at ₹14,550 per gram equivalent because of a demand-supply situation. When your FoF invests your SIP money, it buys at ₹14,550, not at ₹14,461. You are paying ₹89 more per gram than gold is actually worth. This premium flows into your NAV and affects your returns. The reverse happens too. Just note.
On top of this, you pay two layers of expenses. The FoF has its own expense ratio, and the underlying ETF also has one.
In India, gold FoF expense ratios for direct plans average around 0.20%. This is on top of the underlying ETF’s expense ratio of 0.3% to 0.6%. So your total cost is roughly 0.50% to 0.80% per year, versus 0.30% to 0.50% for a direct ETF.
Unless you are specifically uncomfortable with a demat account, ETFs give you the same exposure at a cheaper price.
Pros: No demat account needed. SIP-friendly. Easy to buy and sell. Available for both gold and silver.
Cons: Tracks the ETF price, not the actual metal price. Higher total expense ratio than a direct ETF. One extra layer between you and the metal.
5. Sovereign Gold Bonds (SGBs)
I am sure most of you already know about SGBs, but let me quickly cover the basics for anyone new, and then get to the interesting part.
Sovereign Gold Bonds are government securities denominated in grams of gold. RBI introduced them in 2015. When you buy one unit, you own the equivalent of one gram of gold. What made SGBs popular is that you get two components: one, your investment moves with the gold price, and two, you earn 2.5% annual interest on the original issue price, paid every six months. Gold appreciation plus interest income on top.
But the government has stopped issuing new SGBs. The last tranche was SGB 2023-24 Series IV in February 2024. After the 2025 Union Budget, Finance Minister Nirmala Sitharaman confirmed there are no plans for fresh issuance.
There are about 45 SGB series currently listed on NSE and BSE, with maturities ranging from 2026 to 2032. You can buy them on the secondary market through your demat account, just like buying a stock.
Now here is the part I want you to pay attention to.
If you go to the NSE website, you can see the prices at which these SGBs trade. Most people compare the SGB price with the spot gold price and decide if it is cheap or expensive. But that comparison is not accurate.
The “dirty price” concept
The price you see on the exchange is not just the gold value. Like any bond, it also reflects the value investors assign to the future interest payments. SGBs are traded on a “dirty price” basis, which means the quoted price includes accrued interest. So comparing the SGB price with the spot gold price is not apples to apples.
One way to estimate whether an SGB is genuinely cheaper than gold is to calculate the present value of its remaining interest payments and subtract that from the trading price.
I ran this analysis for all 45 listed SGBs using NSE data as of July 23, 2026, with the IBJA gold price at ₹14,461 per gram. I used an LLM to calculate the present values at a 6% discount rate.
The result: Almost all of the SGBs were trading at a discount to the gold price after adjusting for the coupons.
The deepest discounts are in the longer-dated SGBs:
The premiums and discounts keep changing; this is just how they looked recently.
But there is a con. When your SGB matures, the redemption price is based on the average gold price around the maturity date. That is what you get. If gold happens to be in a dip on those specific days, you receive the lower amount. You cannot hold on for a few more months and wait for a recovery. The maturity date is fixed.
Tax update from April 1, 2026: if you bought your SGB from the original RBI issuance and hold to the full 8-year maturity, capital gains are still tax-free. But if you buy from the secondary market (which is the only option now), capital gains at maturity are taxable at 12.5% LTCG. The 2.5% interest has always been taxable at your slab rate.
By the way, some interpretations say that SGBs bought on the secondary market still qualify for the capital gains exemption if held until maturity.
Pros: Government-guaranteed. 2.5% annual interest on top of gold returns. Currently trading at a discount to gold on the secondary market.
Cons: Fixed maturity date. Liquidity on the exchange is thin for many series. No fresh issuance. Tax-free maturity benefit now only for original primary subscribers.
6. Electronic Gold Receipts (EGRs)
This is the newest product on the list, and I should say up front: most investing platforms do not provide this facility to investors yet. It is a work in progress. So think of this as something to know about for the future.
An EGR is a SEBI-regulated digital receipt that proves you own physical gold stored in a SEBI-accredited vault. Every EGR has to be backed by actual gold. You can buy and sell EGRs on the exchange through your demat account.
And the big differentiator compared to ETFs: you can take physical delivery of the gold whenever you want.
Just like with ETFs, the price on the exchange depends on buyers and sellers. If liquidity is low, you might pay more than the gold is actually worth. So the same iNAV-checking discipline applies here.
The product is promising, but it needs time for volumes and liquidity to build before it becomes practical for retail use. No silver EGR exists yet.
Pros: SEBI-regulated. Physical delivery option. No expense ratio.
Cons: Not mainstream yet. Liquidity issues similar to those in ETFs may arise if you want to buy and sell on the exchange.
*No GST applies when EGRs are bought or sold on the exchange. However, if you convert your physical gold into EGRs and later reconvert them back into physical gold, the GST treatment remains somewhat unclear.
7. Gold and silver combined FoFs and Multi-Asset Allocation Funds
If you want both gold and silver through a single product, there are mutual fund schemes for that.
Gold and silver combined FoFs invest in both a gold ETF and a silver ETF within one fund. Edelweiss Gold and Silver ETF FoF and Motilal Oswal Gold and Silver ETFs FoF are examples. One investment, one SIP, one folio, both metals.
The gold-to-silver ratio is set by the scheme mandate. You cannot customize it. If you want to set your own ratio, separate gold and silver FoFs give you more control.
Then there are Multi-Asset Allocation Funds. Most of them invest across equity, debt and commodities (gold, silver, or both). SEBI requires at least 10% in at least three asset classes.
The gold and silver allocation in these funds typically ranges from 5% to 20% of the corpus and is managed by the fund manager. You have no control over how much precious metals the fund holds at any point.
Combined FoFs work if you want both metals simply. Multi-asset funds work if you want someone else to handle the overall asset allocation. Neither works if you want a specific, controlled precious metals position.
Pros: Simple way to get both metals or a diversified portfolio in one product. SIP-friendly. No demat needed. Professional allocation management (for multi-asset).
Cons: No control over allocation. Precious metals are a small slice in a multi-asset portfolio. Double layer of costs in FoFs.
Seven routes for owning the two most precious metals of gold and silver. The right one is not about which product is “best.” It is about which one fits the way you actually invest: your account setup, your holding period, your tax situation, and whether you want the metal in your hand or just its price movement in your portfolio.

Let’s go back to February 1, 2021. The finance minister has just finished reading the budget, and the market jumps: the Nifty vaults from 13,634 to 14,281, up 4.7% in a single session, its strongest budget-day reaction in at least a decade.
There was a time when it took a real event to move the market. A central bank would change interest rates, or a finance minister would rise to read the budget, and prices would react. Those moments were scheduled, occasional, and mostly polite.
Lately, the market has changed. A single post from the head of one country, an offhand remark from the leader of another, a flare-up at a border, or even the rumour of a new virus can send prices swinging before the morning coffee has cooled.
But the real damage is rarely the price swing itself. It is what the swing does to us.
Imagine you invested in an index fund in January. By March, your portfolio is down 10%. Yet almost nothing about the companies you own has changed. What has changed is everything around them. Your screen is red. The headlines are grim. Selling suddenly feels like the sensible thing to do.
That is the pattern worth noticing. Markets do not become difficult simply because prices fall. They become difficult because fear rises, making temporary uncertainty feel like permanent damage.
All that swinging has a name: volatility. Better still, it can be measured. In India, that measure is India VIX. It rises when the market expects bigger moves and falls when calmer days are expected. In practice, it is also one of the best gauges of how nervous the market has become.
This week we’ll take volatility apart: what it is, where it shows up, the two forms it takes, and how investors and traders each read it. One idea ties it all together. Prices move every day. Emotions don’t. But when emotions do move, they leave their fingerprints all over volatility.
A number with a shape
Start with India VIX itself, across 2026.
It began the year quiet, drifting near 10, the kind of low reading that shows up when nobody expects much to happen. Then late February brought conflict in West Asia, and the line went almost vertical. By March 30 it reached nearly 29, its highest in a year. The market was braced for large daily swings, and it got them.
Then the long descent. A peace agreement signed on June 17 drained the last of the fear out, and by early July India VIX was back under 12, down close to 60% from the March peak.
That whole arc, the near-vertical climb and the slow bleed back, is fear arriving and then leaving. And here is what the “volatility is gone” story leaves out. Today’s reading is low compared with March. Compared with January, it is still higher. The number fell a long way, but it has not gone back to sleep.
Why the number jumps when the market falls
Volatility measures how much a price moves, not which way it moves. Picture two paths for the Nifty, both starting and ending at the same level. One drifts there gently. The other arrives through a series of sharp swings. They finish at the exact same price, but one was volatile and the other was not. Same destination, very different ride. Volatility is the width of that second path: it says nothing about where you end up, only how bumpy the trip was. When India VIX is high, the market is expecting a wide path. When it is low, a narrow one.
By definition, then, volatility is blind to direction. In real markets, direction and volatility are joined at the hip. Take 2026 a fortnight at a time and set each move in the Nifty beside the move in India VIX. Where the index is red, the fear reading turns green, and where the index rises, the fear reading fades. They run as opposites, panel after panel.
But look closer and the mirror is lopsided. In early March the Nifty fell 4.4% and India VIX jumped 38%. In mid-April the Nifty rose a larger 7.2%, and VIX fell just 33%. A bigger move up drew a smaller response than a smaller move down. This is why VIX is called the fear index and not the movement index. In theory it measures movement in both directions. In practice it leans one way, because we do. We do not weigh gains and losses evenly: a fall of a given size frightens us more than a rise of the same size reassures us. Volatility inherits that lopsidedness, growing loudest on the way down, because that is where the fear lives.
The whole world got scared at once
India’s reading did not spike alone.
Take India VIX, America’s VIX, and Japanese and Australian equivalents, set each to the same starting point so their shapes can be compared, and lay them on top of one another. The striking thing is how little of the story belongs to India. The same late-February jump, the same spring peak, the same summer fade appear on every line.
There are differences in height. India ran hotter at the peak, and by early July America’s reading sat higher than ours. But the shape is shared. Volatility is usually a mood the whole world is in, not a local event. A calm Indian market is generally a calm world, and a frightened one rarely panics by itself.
Smaller company, wilder weather
That shared mood is still one number laid over everything. Zoom back into India and volatility is not a single climate but several, and they turn wilder the further down the market you travel.
Sort the market into its broad size tiers and the pattern is orderly. Among the Nifty 50, the largest and most heavily traded companies, the typical stock’s realized volatility sits near 22%. Step down to the Nifty Next 50 and the middle rises to 28%. The midcaps sit near 30%. The smallcaps near 34%, and their tail runs far higher, with individual names moving at two or three times the pace of a steady large-cap.
The reason is familiar even if the numbers are not. The big names carry the weight of index funds, steady institutional ownership and constant coverage, all of which smooth their path. The smaller a company, the thinner its trading and the larger any single piece of news looms, so its price lurches where a large-cap would drift, and the wildest readings of all tend to belong to whichever small name is caught up in a story of its own. The one volatility figure on the ticker is really a large-cap figure. It describes the calm top of the market well and the restless floor beneath it hardly at all.
Two kinds of volatility
We have treated volatility as one thing. It is really two, and the split lines up almost exactly with how investors and traders each look at the market.
Realized volatility is history. It measures how much a price has already moved, worked out straight from past prices. This is the investor’s version of volatility. It is memory, the size of the last scare, and it shapes how risky the market feels right now. When the January investor watched the portfolio fall and felt the urge to sell, that was realized volatility doing its work, backward-looking and felt as fear.
Implied volatility is expectation. It is worked backwards out of option prices, and it reflects how much the market thinks a price will move from here. This is the trader’s version. It looks forward, and the trader is not really asking how risky the market feels. The trader is asking what that expected movement costs.
Across the Nifty 50, most dots land above the line, with implied volatility sitting a little higher than realized. That tilt is normal: options tend to carry a small premium for the movement that might still come. The outliers tell the sharper story.
WIPRO sits high above the line, its options bracing for a swing far larger than the stock has actually made, the kind of gap a trader would call expensive. INFY sits at the far corner below it: it has moved more than almost anything else in the index lately, yet its options now expect noticeably less, which makes that expected movement look cheap.
Two IT names, opposite readings. That gap from the line, expected minus actual, is what a trader watches most closely. Same number, two readings: to the investor, how frightening things feel; to the trader, whether that fear is worth paying for.
The Closing Bell
“Volatility is low” is a fair description of the market today. It is also the least interesting thing you can say about volatility.
The number has a shape, and the shape follows real events. It ignores direction, yet rises mostly when prices fall. It moves across the whole world at once. It hides enormous variety between individual stocks. And it comes in two forms, one measured and one expected. The figure on the ticker is only the surface. Almost everything worth knowing about volatility is in what that figure is quietly averaging over.
The next time a drawdown has your attention, remember that volatility is shaping what you see and feel. Sometimes the businesses you own carry no real stress of their own. But markets are wired together, and a shock elsewhere in the world, or one large event, can reach your portfolio anyway.
Traders sit on the other side of the same number. A high VIX cheers options sellers, who see the fat premiums that fear puts on the table. But a high reading is also the market bracing for large moves, and if those moves arrive, the loss can run well past the premium collected. The fear that pays the seller is the same fear that can sink them.
Either way, reading volatility well changes the decision in front of you, and learning to see it stock by stock, rather than as a single number on the ticker, is what turns it from background noise into information.
Calm is not the absence of volatility. It is volatility resting at the quiet end of its own range.

Imagine if, every year, petrol prices stayed constant, onions cost the same, and milk prices didn’t rise at all.
A world with 0% price rise sounds like a dream.
But central banks don’t chase this dream of zero inflation. Instead, they chase a world where there’s a little bit of inflation each year.
So here’s what I want to talk about today — what’s the holy grail for inflation?
Because since 2016, India has followed something called Flexible Inflation Targeting , or FIT. What it means is that the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) has an inflation target it has to get right — 4%, with room to drift 2% on either side.
And every five years, the government and the RBI sit down and decide whether we should keep the number or change it. The last time they reviewed it was in March 2026 and looks like they’re happy. Because we’re keeping the 4%, +/- 2% target. At least till March 2031.
But the question is — why 4%? Why not 0%?
Also, has India’s FIT actually worked?
Let’s get into it.
Why not just zero?
On the face of it, a 0% inflation target sounds like the obviously correct one. Isn’t a central bank’s primary job to protect the value of your money? So shouldn’t “no rise in prices, ever” be the gold standard?
Well, no.
And that has a lot to do with something else that central bankers are worried about — a fall in prices, or deflation.
See, if you know your washing machine will be cheaper next year, why buy it today? You wait. Everyone waits. Demand dries up. Companies, staring at falling sales, cut production and lay off workers. Now people have even less money to spend, so they wait even longer to buy anything. Prices fall further. Repeat.
Economists call this a deflationary spiral, and once it gets going, it’s hard to stop. Japan spent the better part of three decades stuck in something close to this.
Also, there’s the monetary lever angle.
If a central bank has to fight an economic slowdown or a recession, they resort to tweaking interest rates to make the economy do its bidding. They cut rates to make borrowing cheaper and get people to spend money.
But interest rates can’t theoretically go below zero (yes, it has happened in the past where you would have paid interest for depositing money in a bank rather than earning it, but that’s only a desperate measure). Economists call this the “ zero lower bound” . Because people can always hoard physical cash (which earns 0%), banks cannot force interest rates into the negative territory without causing mayhem.
And if a central bank targets 0% inflation (subsequently near-zero interest rates too), it’s constantly flirting with the edge of that lower bound, leaving itself almost no room to cut rates when a recession hits.
A little bit of positive inflation is a safety buffer.
Then there’s a nerdier point about wages and employment that a group of economists — Akerlof, Dickens and Perry — made in the 1990s.
The tl;dr version of the paper ( pdf ) is that when a company or an industry faces declining demand, the quick economic fix might be to cut wages. Say by 3% so everyone stays employed. But employers also know cutting pay destroys morale and leads to top talent quitting. And hence, what economists call “downward nominal wage rigidity” comes into play here.
This simply means that it’s tough to reduce nominal wages (wages not adjusted for inflation).
Now think about what could happen at 0% inflation.
If overall inflation is 0%, a company that needs to reduce its labour costs by 3% has only one option and that is to lay people off. They cannot reduce nominal pay and the wage stays artificially high. This could also increase permanent unemployment.
But if an economy has 3% inflation, the company keeps nominal pay constant. The real wage drops by 3% and thus, the labour costs are reduced without any layoffs.
Ergo, unemployment doesn’t shoot up.
And that is why and how the consensus that built up globally, across almost every major central bank, is that a low, positive, and stable rate of inflation beats zero (0) inflation
But why has India chosen 4%?
Let’s rewind to 2013.
Inflation in India was ugly and hovering around 9-10%. Household inflation expectations, essentially what ordinary people believed prices would do, had shot up and stayed up. The currency was under pressure.
It was messy.
So the RBI, which was headed by Raghuram Rajan then, decided to fix India’s monetary policy framework. They set up a committee and tasked it with figuring out what could be done.
Sidenote: This committee was also called the Urjit Patel Committee. Urjit Patel would later succeed Rajan as the RBI Governor in 2016.
And in that report ( pdf ), the committee actually ran the numbers to figure out what India’s “right” inflation number should be.
First, they estimated the level of inflation above which growth actually starts getting hurt. That threshold came out to about 6.2%.
Second, they looked back at the mid-2000s (2003-04 to 2006-07), a period when India’s economy was running close to its full potential, neither overheating nor underperforming, and found that inflation during that “just right” period averaged around 4%.
So that set the tone — 4% as a starting point, 6% as the ceiling.
Also, you should know that advanced economies like the US, UK, and the Eurozone typically treat 1-3% inflation as their version of price stability. But emerging economies, from Eastern Europe to Latin America, have historically found that a 4-5% range is what corresponds to genuine price stability for them . This isn’t arbitrary. Emerging economies are still catching up in productivity, they have larger informal sectors, and their price data itself is patchier and gets revised more. A slightly higher target gives you breathing room against that kind of statistical noise.
There’s also India’s specific inflation basket to consider. Food and fuel used to make up ~50% of India’s CPI basket — categories that are hostage to a bad monsoon, a spike in global crude, or a poor harvest, none of which the RBI’s interest rate decisions have much control over. Setting the target too tight, too close to zero, means the RBI would be constantly “failing” its own mandate over things it can’t influence, purely due to one bad monsoon season.
That’s also why there’s a band and not just a single number. The +/-2% cushion exists specifically to absorb these kinds of supply shocks without the RBI needing to panic-react every single quarter.
Did FIT work in India?
Here’s where we need to be careful, because this is exactly the kind of question where it’s tempting to look at a “before” and “after” chart and declare victory.
Because the facts on the “before and after” are quite exciting. Average inflation was around 8% in the decade before FIT was adopted. Since 2016, it has averaged ~4.8%. Inflation volatility has come down.
Source: RBI
Also, economists Barry Eichengreen, Poonam Gupta, and Rishabh Choudhary, ran the numbers for the World Bank ( pdf ) and found that, statistically, actual inflation now has a noticeably smaller effect on shaping people’s future inflation expectations than it used to. In plain English: when prices spike today, people are less likely to assume prices will keep spiking tomorrow. That’s the textbook definition of an “anchor” doing its job. caption...
They say,
Evidence points to improved outcomes: inflation is lower and less volatile; inflation expectations are better anchored; and the transmission of monetary policy is more effective.
But correlation isn’t causation. Which means just because inflation has tempered down since the adoption of FIT, we cannot quite declare it the sole reason for that.
And that’s where an RBI bulletin from July 2025 adds nuance.
Rather than claiming total victory. It found that FIT has genuinely helped anchor expectations, but it was one ingredient among several. Timely government interventions, like export bans on certain foods or cuts to import duties, and a broader period of moderating global prices, worked alongside the monetary framework, not despite it.
So where does that leave us?
Not with a clean, one-line verdict, and if anyone gives you one, be suspicious. The honest answer is: FIT appears to have done real, measurable work in anchoring expectations and improving policy credibility, but it operated inside a decade that was also unusually kind on the oil-price and global-inflation front.
Both things can be true at once.
PS: Did you know that New Zealand was the first country to implement inflation targeting (IT) in 1990? Today, 48 countries have IT as their monetary policy framework.

The market has never been short of surprises. Since 2020, we’ve seen a pandemic, wars, sharp turns in interest rates, and countless earnings announcements that sent individual stocks soaring or sinking overnight. Looking back, those moves seem obvious. What is easier to miss is that, before the news even arrived, the options market was already behaving differently. Not because anyone knew what would happen, but because it was reacting to uncertainty itself.
This brings us to the quiet period just before a company reports its quarterly earnings. In these final days, because the direction of the news is genuinely unknown, the share price has little reason to drift and often stays fairly still. Yet, beneath this calm surface, the options market is anything but quiet. Both the call, which pays off if the stock rises, and the put, which pays off if it falls, become more expensive at the same time. The market is quietly bracing for a large move without betting on its direction. The uncertainty missing from the share price has simply moved into the options.
Wipro’s pre-earnings price action shows this perfectly. Before its results, the stock usually stays within its recent range, giving away very little. But after the results are announced, every quarter looks different. Some announcements barely move the stock, while others send it dramatically higher or lower. The evening before gives no clue which kind of quarter this will be, which is precisely the mystery the options market tries to price.
Expectation vs. Reality
Before we can understand what the options market was forecasting for Wipro, it helps to look at what had actually been happening. The year 2026 had been volatile, with wars, trade tariffs, and foreign investors pulling money out of Indian stocks all pushing prices around. This brings us to a key concept: realized volatility. It simply measures how much a stock has actually moved in the recent past.
Wipro’s stock reflected this story. While it had periods of relative calm, its price swung twice pushing its realized volatility from around 20% to nearly 40%. If realized volatility is the story of movement that has already happened, implied volatility (IV) is the market’s expectation of future movement. It is the number at the heart of our pre-earnings mystery, reflecting how much of a price swing the options market is anticipating before a particular option expires.
Reading the Forecast
But a number like implied volatility means very little until you know what is normal. An IV of 40% could be unusually high for one stock but completely normal for another. This is why traders don’t just look at IV; they look at the Implied Volatility Percentile (IVP). IVP compares today’s IV with the stock’s own IV over the past year, giving it a score from 0 to 100. A reading of 90 means today’s IV is higher than it was on 90% of trading days over the last year, signaling that the market’s expectation for movement is unusually high.
The difference between IV and IVP is critical. Consider Adani Power and Adani Ports. They have almost the same implied volatility, around 38-39%. But their IV Percentiles tell opposite stories. Adani Power’s IVP of 9 shows its current IV is among the lowest it has been all year. Meanwhile, Adani Ports has an IVP of 95, meaning its IV is near a yearly high. The market is pricing in far more uncertainty for Adani Ports, a context only IVP can reveal. Looking at the table, you’ll notice many stocks with the highest IVP are, unsurprisingly, just days away from their earnings announcements.
The Storm That Never Came
Now, let’s apply this lens to Wipro. In the run-up to its results, its implied volatility climbed to about 41%, pushing its IV Percentile to 95. The market was clearly expecting a much larger move than usual. This is the moment some traders wait for. They see a high IVP and believe the market has priced in too much uncertainty. Their strategy is to sell both the call and the put, collecting the high premiums while betting the actual stock move will be less dramatic than expected.
Notice what happened the moment Wipro announced its results. Implied volatility fell sharply, dropping from 41% to the mid-twenties in a single session. This is the IV crush. An option works a little like insurance: it costs more when a storm is in the forecast and less once the sky has cleared, because what you are really paying for is the uncertainty, not the storm itself. Once the result was out, that uncertainty was gone, and the inflated premiums went with it, whichever way the news broke.
On the evening before its results, the options market had priced in an expected move of about 5.9%, creating a breakeven range for the seller of both the at-the-money call and put options between 167.3 and 188.2. As it turned out, Wipro rose only about 1.9%, finishing the month near 181. The stock stayed well within the range the options market had priced in. The trader who recognized that the market had priced in more fear than the event eventually delivered came out ahead, not by predicting the news, but by correctly judging the market’s overestimation of the move.
When the Storm Comes Anyway
But this strategy doesn’t always work. Wipro is only half the story. TCS, which reported its earnings earlier, shows what happens when the market’s expectations are too low. Before its results, the options market priced an expected move of about 6.2%. A trader selling those at-the-money call and put options together might have concluded, just as with Wipro, that the market was expecting too much.
This time, they would have been wrong. Once TCS announced its results, the stock moved well beyond the 6.2% range, pushing past the breakeven levels and into a loss for the seller. That is the risk. A buyer of an option can only lose the premium paid, but a seller’s losses can keep growing if the stock moves much further than expected. The same approach that worked on Wipro failed on TCS.
The Closing Bell
The key lesson is this: implied volatility is a powerful tool for understanding how much movement the market is expecting, and IV Percentile tells you whether that expectation is unusually high or low for a particular stock. But neither is a prediction.
Before an earnings announcement, the options market prices uncertainty into both the call and the put. Once the results are out, that uncertainty vanishes, implied volatility falls, and option premiums fall with it. Traders are not trying to predict the news. They are trying to judge whether the market has priced in too much movement or too little. Implied volatility does not tell you what will happen. It tells you what the market expects to happen. Understanding that difference is the first step to understanding how options are priced.
